title: Transport minister won't change mind on controversial Matilda Bay ferry terminal
text:
WA's transport minister has insisted she will not change her mind about the location of a controversial new ferry terminal at Matilda Bay, despite growing community backlash and projected cost blowouts.

The WA government promised to expand Metronet ferry services on Perth's Swan River during the 2025 state election campaign, at a joint Commonwealth-state cost of $107 million.

Two new ferry terminals were proposed, one at Applecross and one at Matilda Bay in Nedlands — directly opposite the University of Western Australia — to be serviced by five new electric ferries.

Rita Saffioti says Matilda Bay is simply the best choice for the Nedlands terminal. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Today the government confirmed the cost of the whole project had increased to about $150 million.

Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said the Matilda Bay section had incurred increased costs to "change the nature of the jetty and the length of the jetty"

Locals upset

The Western Australian Planning Commission approved the development for the new ferry terminals last December, but the government has continued to face opposition from locals, the Liberals and the Greens.

A petition tabled in WA's parliament today, signed by over 10,000 people, called for construction contracts to be suspended so more analysis of the Matilda Bay site could take place.

Ms Saffioti said a comprehensive analysis of five key sites in Nedlands had deemed Matilda Bay the best.

"We made a commitment at the election, we then went back and assessed all the different options again," Ms Saffioti said.

Row over plan for ferry terminal at Perth's Matilda Bay deepens A WA government-commissioned analysis finds the scenic and popular Matilda Bay is the safest spot for a ferry terminal, just as another report prompted by an advocacy group says it would put river users at serious risk.

She said "environmental experts" found alternative sites including Jojo's and Pelican Point were not suitable "because of the impact on seagrass, migratory birds and also impacts into some reserves".

Asked if the ferry site would be moved, Ms Saffioti said she was "not going to change [her] mind".

"There's no reason for me not to choose a better site if a better site was told to me," she said.

" It's not as if I'm just captured by this site, I took the advice. "

Save Matilda Bay spokesperson Megan Bagworth said her group would continue to lobby for the Nedlands ferry landing to be moved to Jojo's.

"Once it's built, it can't be undone," Ms Bagworth said.

"That's why the government needs to do the full and proper assessments now and review this decision."

'Yet another blowout'

Opposition transport spokesperson Steve Martin said Ms Saffioti had "blown another budget" at a time of cost-of-living pressures for West Australians.

Steve Martin is criticising the government for another cost blowout. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"Here we are, yet another blowout on the top of the Fremantle Traffic Bridge [Walyalup Bridge] that went from $230 million to $596 million and counting," he said.

Construction on the ferry terminals is expected to commence in coming weeks, with the ferry services expected to start in late 2027.

title: Science cancelled and class numbers doubled as mouldy classrooms in WA shut
text:
Class sizes at a Wheatbelt school have doubled this term after mould forced part of the campus to close.

Five classrooms and a toilet block at Lancelin Primary School have been closed for nearly seven weeks, forcing multiple classes to share rooms and science lessons replaced with sport.

A longstanding issue

Parents and Community Association president and mother to two students, Jade Hamlyn said the school, 125 kilometres north of Perth, has about 150 students split between seven core classrooms.

Water damage is visible outside a classroom. (Supplied: Shane Love)

She said authorities had known about a recurring mould issue for more than a decade, and she could not believe it had been neglected to the point of closing facilities.

"It's appalling that the school and the school staff have had to advocate for 14 years to get anything to be done," Ms Hamlyn said.

She said many parents had health concerns.

"My daughter actually has been quite ill in regards to respiratory issues.

"Now I'm questioning whether this is a result of [the mould].

" I'd love to ask them [the state government] would you put your child in that classroom? "

Jade Hamlyn has six children, two of whom are currently attending the school and have been affected by the mould issues. (Supplied: Jade Hamyln)

Mixed classes disrupting students

Ms Hamlyn said the closures had forced multiple year groups to share the same rooms.

She said her pre-primary-aged daughter had refused to go to school for three weeks as the cohort shared a class with the kindergartens.

"She's finding that it's just too disruptive … she can't handle having so many students in one room," she said.

Ms Hamlyn said her older daughter in year 6 was learning in the library with another class, along with its regular users.

"There's three classes in this library at any one time," she said.

"You've got two of them actually trying to learn their lessons with book displays as borders [separating classes]."

An outdoor area was also closed during Shane Love's visit to the school. (Supplied: Shane Love)

Ms Hamlyn said science lessons had been replaced with physical education for the rest of the year as the dedicated facility was being used as a regular classroom.

"That's a huge concern because my child's a part of the graduating cohort, which then [science] won't be included in her school report," she said.

Like Ms Hamlyn, school board member and mother of three students, Casey Clarke said sharing classrooms was disruptive.

"There's like 35 to 40 little kids in one classroom," she said.

Ms Clarke said she knew of multiple families considering moving from Lancelin as they no longer wanted to send their children to the school.

"We've just got so many worried families," she said.

It's just a horrible situation."

Not a quick fix

Ms Clarke said staff had logged multiple incident reports to try and get the mould thoroughly removed, but were met with band-aid fixes each time.

"They [the Department of Education] can't have fixed the problem when they're not taking out cupboards or carpets to see the full ramifications of the moisture," she said.

" We are not comfortable to put our kids back into the rooms given they have not been sufficiently cleaned. "

Ms Clarke said her own children had frequent upper respiratory issues, which she thought could be connected to the mould.

Nationals WA member for Mid West Shane Love said the school looked "badly neglected" when he recently visited.

Shane Love says the classrooms' contents have been packed up. (Supplied: Shane Love)

He said the kindergarten classroom was in an "ancient" demountable building which had begun to deteriorate.

"The floor had basically rotted away and was all mouldy," Mr Love said.

He said a group of classrooms had visible water damage on their ceilings, and the pre-primary classroom's verandah had been cordoned off as it was mouldy.

"The department is saying that there's water damage. There's a bit more than water damage; you could smell the mould in there, Mr Love said.

"To have allowed this situation to develop, I think, is reprehensible by the Department [of Education]."

'Lessons continued as normal'

The Department of Education confirmed five classrooms were closed in October to inspect and repair moisture damage.

"Lessons continued as normal with students being accommodated in the school library and science room," a spokesperson said.

In November, four of the rooms were declared safe, but the school principal kept them closed for "unrelated work," including window cleaning, painting and installing new carpet.

The spokesperson said the fifth classroom would be replaced with a new transportable building next year due to a flooring issue.

They said the girls' toilets were closed as a precaution while contractors investigated potential water damage, but other facilities were available.

title: Gas reservation scheme set to pass parliament in bid to rein in energy costs
text:
Australia will have a domestic gas reservation scheme to shore up local supplies and drive down prices more than a decade after the emergence of a lucrative export industry sent costs soaring for households and manufacturers.

A deal between Labor and the Coalition to support the scheme has not been formally confirmed, but the legislation is expected to pass the Senate tonight after the opposition indicated it would not oppose it.

Under the plan, the federal government would require gas exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their exports for domestic use from 2028 to reduce energy prices and stem the loss of Australian manufacturing.

Gas policy feud The federal government's push for a gas reserve looks likely to succeed, but it has revealed a bitter split between major gas companies.

The Coalition's confirmation it would not vote against the bill followed an agreement between the federal and Western Australian governments to exempt that state from the national scheme.

WA has had its own gas reservation policy for two decades, which has helped to insulate its economy from the price shocks experienced on the east coast.

East coast gas market catches up to west

Resources Minister Madeleine King said the reservation would create a permanent buffer between international gas prices and the Australian domestic market.

"What should have been done years ago is being delivered by this government for the Australian people," she said.

"Australia's national gas reservation scheme will create an enduring framework that brings to an end over a decade of crisis-driven ad hoc market interventions."

Madeleine King says the policy will create an enduring framework that will stop crisis-driven market interventions. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Reserve Bank analysis in 2021 found wholesale gas prices outside WA had roughly doubled following Queensland's liquefied natural gas exports in 2015, while prices in the west had been about half those paid in the eastern states.

The disparity has persisted, with WA recording an average domestic gas price of $7.45 a gigajoule in 2024-25, while east coast buyers have been signing long-term contracts at about $12 to $13 a gigajoule, according to the latest figures from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

The intervening years have also seen the closure of major Australian manufacturing plants, with the cost and availability of gas cited as contributing factors in the demise of plastics manufacturer Qenos and Incitec Pivot's Gibson Island fertiliser plant in Brisbane.

Coalition seeks investment safeguards

Shadow Resources Minister Susan McDonald told the Senate the opposition would not block Labor's reforms despite the opposition's lingering concerns about their potential to discourage investment in new gas projects.

"We will not oppose this legislation because we want reliable and affordable gas for Australians," she said.

"We want more gas production and policies that encourage more investment."

The Coalition has sought several changes to the scheme, including doubling the proportion of an exporter's domestic supply obligation that can be deferred from 10 to 20 per cent.

Under Labor's proposal, the domestic market would be deliberately oversupplied to put downward pressure on prices.

Susan McDonald has expressed concerns about the changes discouraging investment in new gas projects. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The opposition has pushed for the government to have greater flexibility in determining the extent of that surplus, rather than automatically targeting an oversupply of 10 per cent.

It also wanted the government to take into account the long-term cost of producing gas and the need to encourage new investment when making those decisions.

But the amendments would not require the government to achieve a particular wholesale price.

'Santos' loopholes threaten gas plan Industry players and observers say draft gas reservation plans are full of carve-outs that will let one company off the hook.

The Coalition has also proposed safeguards for WA's exemption, including preventing it from automatically expiring and limiting the circumstances in which a future federal minister could revoke it.

The Greens have criticised the expected agreement between the major parties, arguing a tax on gas exports would deliver a better return to Australians from the sale of the nation's natural resources.

"We know the core national reforms needed when it comes to gas. It's an export gas tax," Greens leader David Shoebridge said.

"A 25 per cent minimum would put $17 billion on the table."

title: Returning Matildas star Cooney-Cross wants to make late mum 'proud'
text:
When Kyra Cooney-Cross returned to the pitch for Arsenal in the Women's Super League in September, she shared a moving message from her mum.

Its essence is one that so many parents would have relayed to their kids in one manner or another in their sporting careers, whether they were as decorated as a Matildas' linchpin, or finding their feet for the first time in the under 5s.

"Kyra, try to remember what it felt like when you were little … when you just loved having the ball at your feet, playing with your mates, testing yourself against the boys or adults for the fun of it," the message read.

"Play because you love the ball at your feet, the rhythm of the game. Train because it feels good to move and challenge your body and feel strong.

"This is how you start doing it for you again — Mum."

Amongst the pain of losing her mother Jess to terminal bile duct cancer in July, Cooney-Cross has taken the message to heart, and three months after returning to club football, she's back for the Matildas.

Kyra Cooney-Cross returned for her club side Arsenal in August. (Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

The 24-year-old is in the squad for friendlies against Colombia in Canberra and Geelong, in a key test just seven months out from the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

"It's bittersweet. It's my first time back with the national team since everything that's happened with my mum and our family," she told ABC News Breakfast.

"But playing for your country, this is the highest level I can play at, and it's the highest level I can make my mum proud.

"So I'm really looking forward to it and being back at home in Geelong in front of my family and friends and just being back with the team."

Cooney-Cross last played for the Matildas at the Women's Asian Cup in March. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

Cooney-Cross's last international appearance was in March's Women's Asian Cup, and after her breakthrough tournament at the now fabled 2023 World Cup, she's eager to recreate those highs.

"It's definitely flown by. I don't think a lot of us players had even the time to process the World Cup and what we had done in this country and for women's football in Australia," she said.

"We're just going to work really hard. Stick together and focus on these next two games.

"The World Cup is obviously really important and we want to get really far."

McKenna making moves

Cooney-Cross will play a pivotal part in Brazil next year but others on the fringe, like midfielder Leticia McKenna, hope for their own breakout moment.

Leticia McKenna made her Matildas debut earlier this year. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

McKenna, 24, made her international debut in April, and starred for Melbourne City before securing a move to Nottingham Forest in the second tier of English women's football.

She was also recently named PFA Young Footballer of the Year.

"It's been very surreal. It's been a really big year, something I'm extremely proud of," she said.

McKenna's UK move made waves, setting an A-League Women's record with her transfer fee.

"It was a very, very hard decision to leave. It came up at quite short notice as well and I was very happy at the position I was in with Melbourne City and I was looking forward to the upcoming season in that regard," she said.

"But it was something I felt I was ready for. It was always in the back of my mind to make that step and move overseas."

Having made the most of her opportunities with the national side so far, and with only a handful of games left in the lead up, McKenna is eyeing off a berth in that final World Cup squad.

"You always gotta have a goal and aspirations and it's always been a dream," she said.

"Super grateful to be here and it's just making me even hungrier to keep dreaming."

title: Coalition plan to partly privatise Melbourne's sewerage system if elected
text:
Opposition Leader Jess Wilson will partly privatise Melbourne's sewerage network, cut and delay level crossing removals and walk back Labor plans to expand free kindergarten if elected on Saturday.

Ms Wilson, who is also the shadow treasurer, defended releasing the policies more than a week after early voting opened. More than 1.6 million Victorians have already voted.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

"That's a matter for Victorians," Ms Wilson said, two days before the election.

"Victorians decide when they vote and decide why they vote and with the information that they have at that time.

"We're releasing them in full for Victorians today."

Recycled sewage treatment privatisation policy promises savings

The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) tallied up the cost of Ms Wilson's policies, finding that net debt would be $20 billion lower over four years under the Coalition, down to $176 billion. This would also reduce the Victorian interest bill.

The main benefit to the budget is leasing Melbourne Water's Eastern and Western sewage treatment plants under the "asset recycling program". This would add $13.63 billion to state coffers by 2030-31, including land sales.

The Coalition has taken this policy to its last two elections.

Plans to lease sewage treatment plants are a significant source of savings in the Coalition's costings. (Supplied: David Mullins)

Ms Wilson in August said she "wouldn't touch" Melbourne Water when pressed on whether it could be privatised, and on Thursday rejected that a long-term lease amounted to privatisation. Labor has previously looked at privatising the assets.

Ms Wilson insisted that household water bills would not go up under the model, despite a poor track record of privatising the sewerage network overseas.

Environmental group Clean Ocean Foundation expressed alarm over the proposal, arguing the part-privatisation presented a "clear and present danger to Victoria's coastlines, rivers and waterways".

"Wastewater treatment is not simply an infrastructure investment opportunity; it is a critical environmental safeguard," the group said.

"Private operators have commercial incentives that may conflict with the public interest, particularly when it comes to costly treatment upgrades, emerging contaminants, nutrient removal and pollution prevention.

"We cannot afford to compromise environmental standards or allow the pursuit of private returns to come at the expense of the health of our marine and freshwater environments."

Change of plans for free kinder, level crossing upgrade plans

Ms Wilson also revealed that a Coalition government would not expand free kindergarten to 30 hours a week for four-year-olds, up from 15 hours, as is existing Labor government policy.

"We will also guarantee free kinder in a responsible and disciplined fashion by making the scheme sustainable," she said.

" By keeping the rollout at 15 hours per week, we can guarantee free kinder in the future. "

The Coalition was looking to allow providers to charge a gap fee under the "free kinder" model, but Ms Wilson ruled that out on Thursday.

Plans for free kinder and level crossings would change if the Coalition wins the state election. (AAP: James Ross)

If elected, Ms Wilson said her government would also cancel the level crossing removals in Yarraville, Spotswood, and all those along the Upfield line in Brunswick and Parkville.

Level crossing removals in Seaford would be delayed beyond 2030.

Yarraville and Spotswood are already contracted, which Ms Wilson said would cost $90 million to break, ultimately saving $2.127 billion. Of that, $1.2 billion is within the forward estimates.

She also weakened her commitment to reach a cash surplus by 2032, clarifying that this was the 2033 financial year.

Economists have previously doubted the Coalition's ability to reach the commitment, a critique seized upon by Labor.

Road maintenance investment boost, as public service spend drops

Ms Wilson has relied on her plan to reduce the Victorian Public Service (VPS) through attrition — estimated to save $5.69 billion by 2030-31 — would help reach that goal.

Nationals leader Danny O'Brien said the Transport Accident Commission (TAC) scheme was over-funded, which would be re-invested in road maintenance.

The PBO expects this measure to save about $3.4 billion over the forward estimates.

But independent economist Saul Eslake cautioned that it could result in "compulsory third-party insurance premiums going up by more than they might otherwise".

"That hasn't been spelled out in the document," he said.

Ms Wilson had been under pressure to explain how she would reduce debt while promising to spend more than Labor and cutting taxes.

Jess Wilson has been under pressure to release the Coalition's costings. (ABC News)

The PBO costings said expenditure under the Coalition would reduce by $3.246 billion over four years, while revenue would reduce by $590.9 million.

The Coalition would draw down $5.734 billion from unallocated contingency funding, set aside for unexpected costs, to pay off debt.

" There is emergency contingency funds that remain," Ms Wilson said. "This is unallocated contingencies. "

The Coalition has counted on selling renewable energy projects owned by the State Electricity Commission (SEC) to gain $1 billion, including battery projects and the Delburn Wind Farm.

The contentious Suburban Rail Loop factors into questions about the Coalition's costings. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Ms Wilson insisted that pausing and reviewing the $35 billion SRL East rail line between Cheltenham and Box Hill will not have an impact on the budget, given she said she would continue work on all existing contracts.

"We don't know the contracts for the SRL," she said.

The Coalition would also sell the air rights to the Richmond station precinct.

Measures lack 'tough decisions'

The question of how the opposition would fund promises to both cut taxes and create new spending measures has loomed over the election campaign.

RMIT public policy professor David Hayward said today's announcements identified where the money would come from, but a lack of "tough decisions" could create fiscal headaches in the future.

"Economist will say more needs to be done to get the budget under control, and selling assets to pay down debt is a temporary fix rather than a long-term one," he said.

Labor was highly critical of the Coalition's plans while releasing its own costings, particularly Ms Wilson's plans for the sewerage system.

"To dump this out two days before the election shows a level of cynicism that means she does not deserve to be premier," Treasurer Colin Brooks said.

"You cannot mislead people this way and expect to be elected premier."

Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the Liberals' plan to partly privatise the sewerage system "frankly stinks".

"It will be a disaster and lead to skyrocketing bills just like it did in the UK," Ms Sandell said.

title: Why the US Army detonated tonnes of toxic chemical near farmland
text:
The US Army has destroyed America's entire stockpile of a toxic bomb-making material in a controlled explosion in Iowa.

The detonation took place at 9am on Wednesday, local time, in Middletown, Iowa, following a public outcry.

Here's what to know about the operation.

Why was the stockpile blown up?

In 2009, stockpiles of lead azide (an explosive chemical once used to detonate military munitions) were moved from military bases across the country to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for long-term storage.

US detonates lead azide explosives Residents in the area are being urged to take precautions due to concerns the explosion may throw lead particles into the air.

The army said in March it had discovered the lead azide had crystallised and become unstable.

Officials said the compound would eventually explode on its own if left unaddressed, and chemically neutralising or relocating the storage drums was not possible.

With winter approaching, the army said the situation was becoming more urgent, as cold temperatures risked a spontaneous explosion.

Leaders decided a controlled detonation of the more than four tonnes of chemical was the safest course of action.

Why were people concerned?

The detonation was likely to create a plume of lead-laced dust that could travel up to 80 kilometres south-west of the military installation, reaching the north-east corner of neighbouring Missouri.

The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. (AP: Austin Johnson)

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that can cause long-term health problems in humans and animals.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa, said there is no safe level of exposure, particularly for children and pregnant people, because lead can inhibit brain development and impair cognitive abilities.

Environmental groups had sued to block the explosion, and although it was temporarily halted by orders from an appeals court and US President Donald Trump, it was ultimately allowed to go ahead.

Dr O'Shaughnessy said immediate risks from inhaling the lead particles would likely be mitigated if people sheltered from the dust plume as it passed over them.

Nearby towns were voluntarily evacuated ahead of the detonation, and residents in wider affected areas were advised to keep their windows and doors closed for 24-48 hours after the detonation.

But Dr O'Shaughnessy said long-term risks could come from lead dust settling on homes, farms and in the environment, where it would not break down further.

The blast sent plumes of white smoke into the sky. (Reuters: Jim Urquhart)

Iowa is one of the US's biggest farming states, with agriculture estimated to make up about 20 per cent of its economy.

Officials estimated about 350 farms could be impacted by the fallout.

Farmers and ranchers worried about protecting their crops and herds.

While the state's Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship recommended cattle farmers move their livestock, feed and equipment to alternate locations or indoors to avoid direct exposure, it acknowledged that in some places, that would not be feasible.

"I don't think lead danger goes away any time soon," said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington.

"It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this."

Was the detonation contained?

To contain the blast, earthen barriers were built around a pair of bunkers containing 68 barrels of lead azide.

Foam and water were used to tamp down any dust, as witnesses reported two white plumes billowing high into the air before quickly dissipating.

The Environmental Protection Agency said in a statement following the detonation that its air monitors had detected no airborne lead throughout the region.

A NASA research aircraft was seen circling the area after the detonation. (AP: Austin Johnson)

But researchers said the final results aren't in yet.

Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University, said while the early results were promising, samples still needed to determine whether there were any health risks.

"This should take days to weeks," he said.

The EPA said it would test air, land and water samples in the coming days and deploy remediation efforts "where necessary".

But some residents told Reuters they had gathered their own soil samples for independent testing.

Doug Seyb, a livestock farmer from Donnellson, was still concerned about the accuracy of EPA air monitors.

"All of these cows are pregnant, and we just cross our fingers that we don't have deformed calves and stillborns," he said.

Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand said he was grateful to experts for limiting the lead dispersal, but the lead-up "should never have been so chaotic and unclear".

"Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared," he said.

"There must be immediate transparency to understand how and why this situation became what it did."

ABC/AP/Reuters

title: ASIC sues major insurer over complaints handling and claims delays
text:
The corporate regulator is suing major insurer AIG over its handling of hundreds of customer complaints about general insurance claims.

ASIC alleges AIG Australia, which offers travel insurance and consumer device insurance, failed to provide complaint responses or delay notifications within the required 30-day timeframe in 534 cases.

Some customers waited for months for complaint decisions, including those who were unwell, injured or recently bereaved, between October 2021 and December 2025.

ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said policyholders should not have to fight their insurer for basic communication.

"Making a complaint to your insurer should be a pathway to resolving a problem, not the beginning of another one," he said.

Mr Kirkland alleged some customers were also given inaccurate explanations for the delays.

"Complaint handling is a fundamental obligation for insurers, who must take complaints seriously," he said.

Alan Kirkland says insurers need to take complaints seriously. (ABC News: Adam Wyatt)

"Insurers must have effective systems for recording complaints and should not have to search personal drives and emails to know whether a complaint was responded to."

ASIC alleged the delays caused uncertainty, frustration and emotional distress, and that some customers faced delays receiving insurance payments, refunds or compensation.

AIG Australia is a publicly listed subsidiary of the global American International Group, headquartered in New York.

The parent company saw a net income of $US3.1 billion in the 2025 financial year.

In a statement to the ABC, an AIG spokesperson said it acknowledged the enforcement action.

"We are considering the claim carefully and continue to liaise with ASIC," the spokesperson said.

"AIG Australia continues to make significant improvements to our IDR (internal dispute resolution) processes and remain firmly committed to delivering fair and timely outcomes for our customers."

AIG is a prominent sponsor of women's golf. (Getty Images: Andrew Redington)

Automated 'complexity' excuse

The corporate regulator also alleged AIG used a standard template for communications about delays that pre-populated "complexity" as the reason for the delay, and failed to inform customers of their rights to escalate complaints to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

ASIC alleged the insurer failed to have an effective system for recording information about complaints and keeping track of their progress.

This system did not provide an alert when a complaint response was due, or reliably record whether complaints had been answered.

The news comes weeks after the federal court fined insurance giant Hollard $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable.

ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof.

The outcome was the first civil penalty ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith.

Hollard admitted contravening the Insurance Contracts Act.

Loading...

ASIC put insurers on notice

In December 2024, ASIC put general insurers on notice after a review of 11 insurers found they failed to identify one in six complaints, alongside shortcomings in customer communications, complaints-handling systems and the identification of systemic issues.

"ASIC has put insurers on notice about complaints-handling failures. Those that continue to fall short of their legal obligations should expect enforcement action," Mr Kirkland said.

ASIC said it was seeking declarations, pecuniary penalties, adverse publicity orders and orders requiring AIG to engage an independent expert to review its complaints-handling arrangements and implement recommendations.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this investigation, you can securely contact reporter Adelaide Miller at miller.adelaide@proton.me

The enforcement action also comes as the Insurance Council of Australia's redrafted code of practice is under review by ASIC.

The corporate regulator is seeking public feedback on the redrafted code, before deciding whether to approve to proposed changes.

NRL boss Peter V’landys has raised concerns about the owner of Wests Tigers investing in soccer rather than rugby league as the cross-code venture sparks a new round of boardroom turmoil. The move into the round-ball game by the Holman Barnes Group is the subject of internal tension at the $100 million leagues club empire, which has a 90 per cent stake in the Wests Tigers and controls the NRL team’s board. Loading In the latest flare-up, deputy chairman Frank Primerano was one of two HBG directors to have his membership suspended on Tuesday night over undisclosed disciplinary charges. One of the main drivers of HBG’s decision to buy a minority shareholding in A-League men’s team Central Coast Mariners and take over operations of the Mariners’ women’s team, Primerano had last week been removed from the Tigers board, where he served as deputy to chairman Barry O’Farrell and had been a central player in the re-signing of coach Benji Marshall until 2030.

The suspension is an interim step only and is not a finding of wrongdoing. A suspension of membership does not of itself result in a vacation of office or end a person’s directorship,” the statement said. NRL boss Peter V’landys. It is unclear what they are alleged to have done but Primerano has been heavily involved in the shift into soccer, in which he was a long-time administrator.

The Tigers owner’s foray into another sport has grabbed the attention of V’landys, who brought it up during a meeting with NRL club chiefs in Sydney on Wednesday. Chairman Dennis Burgess said three months ago that branching out into soccer was part of a strategy of “broadening our sporting footprint”. Hundreds of home buyers of two major property developments, one each in Dee Why and Blacktown, have been left in limbo as nearly $20 million they paid in deposits has gone missing, and the solicitor at the centre of the fiasco has had his legal licence suspended. Lawyer Ken Neville at Branston Neville Lawyers has been suspended by the Law Society pending court proceedings. Solicitor Ken Mark Neville and his Bella Vista-based law firm Branston Neville Lawyers are being pursued through the Supreme Court by developer Landmark Group amid allegations the home buyer deposits on 285 units remain unaccounted for from the firm’s trust account. Justice Anthony McGrath has ordered an account of the project’s funds by Neville, and for the funds to be transferred to a new trust account. An emergency council meeting of the Law Society of NSW was called late on Thursday afternoon at which Neville’s legal licence was suspended and a manager appointed to take control of the practice with immediate effect.

Advertisement

“As this matter may be the subject of further investigation, and with related matters presently before the court, any further comment at this time would be inappropriate,” a spokesperson for the Law Society said. Of the estimated 285 buyers affected by the missing deposits, about half are in the Dee Why development called Casa Delmar, where buyers were due to settle this week. Among them is Lobsang Thupten, a 48-year-old refugee from Tibet who took the day off work on Thursday to take possession of his newly built first home. Instead, the gyprocker, from TB Yak Plastering, is left wondering what will happen to his deposit on the nearly $1.5 million apartment and when he’ll be able to move in. Lobsang Thupten outside the Dee Why apartment he was due to settle on Thursday. Janie Barrett A spokesperson for Landmark Group said no purchaser had been asked to pay their deposit again, and the solicitors of affected purchasers had been advised. Landmark is yet to confirm the revised settlement date.

Advertisement

According to a source familiar with the operations at Landmark Group, more than $24 million in deposits were held in the trust account of Branston Neville Lawyers from 285 unit sales in the Casa Delmar development at Dee Why and the Second Avenue development at Blacktown. However, when the developer changed law firms a few months ago, only about $5 million of those deposits were transferred to the trust account of their newly appointed law firm Hendrix Legal. The Delmar development at Dee Why. Janie Barrett When the deposits were not transferred, Landmark reported the matter to the Law Society of NSW and commenced proceedings in the Supreme Court. A Landmark spokesperson said freeze orders had been issued against the firm and its principal’s bank accounts. Arash Tavakoli, who heads Landmark Group, issued a statement on Thursday saying he was dismayed by the situation, particularly for first home buyers and families who had planned to move in before Christmas.

Advertisement

“[Buyers] did everything right,” Tavakoli said. “They paid their deposits into a solicitor’s trust account, which should be the safest place their money could be. We are committed to every one of these sales, and we will keep fighting until every deposit is accounted for.” Casa Delmar is a complex of 288 apartments, almost all of which had sold before the project was completed. Of those, about 140 sales are affected by the missing deposit funds. The 21-storey development at Blacktown is almost complete and almost entirely sold. Of its 343 apartments, 145 apartments are affected. Of the 343 apartments in Landmark’s Second Avenue development at Blacktown, about 145 apartments are affected by the missing deposit funds. Lauren Sudol, 28, bought her one-bedroom-plus study in Casa Delmar three years ago, only to discover hours before she was due to settle that her deposit money was missing.

Advertisement

“On the day I was due to settle, I woke up with my family celebrating ‘settlement day’ on my first home,” said Sudol, a real estate agent for the past 10 years at Stone Real Estate. “I’m baffled and severely disappointed at the lack of accountability over these deposits held by the law firm. In real estate we are so accountable in terms of how trust accounts are managed.” First home buyer Lauren Sodol is outraged after her deposit went missing. Domain Landmark Group is expected to ask the Law Society of NSW to cover outstanding costs via its compensation fund. The fund is capped at $1 million payable on all claims against a law firm. “People are understandably extremely distressed the deposits they have worked so hard to save have gone missing,” a spokesperson for the NSW government said. “This a serious matter which is before the courts and we hope it can be resolved as quickly as possible.”

Advertisement

NSW Police are aware of the matter. “Investors will also have mounting costs as they will be unable to rent out apartments,” Winning said. Former housing minister Mick de Brenni was effectively “everywhere” in the Queensland Building and Construction Commission’s decision-making, despite no formal ministerial directions ever being issued, an ex-senior building watchdog executive told the CFMEU inquiry on Thursday. Former QBCC licensing director Ian Grant said then-commissioner Brett Bassett described his relationship with de Brenni to him as “one of plausible deniability” – a comment Grant said was made in front of several witnesses. Grant said that culture permeated the upper echelons of the QBCC, in which de Brenni’s name was barely mentioned. Former Labor minister Mick de Brenni. Jamila Filippone Instead, references were made to “the person whose name we cannot mention” and “our political master” – a practice championed by then-deputy commissioner Philip Halton and sometimes adopted by Bassett.

Advertisement

Asked to explain “plausible deniability”, Grant said: “That the minister’s involved, but it’s plausible that you can deny involvement.” “The minister could only direct a commissioner to do something by putting it in writing and tabling it,” he said. “That never occurred, but the minister is everywhere here.” In his witness statement, Grant said Halton, de Brenni’s former chief of staff, advocated wider use of licensing conditions to produce faster regulatory outcomes than traditional enforcement. The most serious allegations centred on a 2019 meeting about possible action against tier-one contractor Watpac, then embroiled in an enterprise bargaining dispute involving the CFMEU and subcontractors over the North Queensland Stadium in Townsville.

Advertisement

Grant said Bassett opened the meeting by saying words to the effect that “the only reason we are here is because an EBA has not been signed”. Grant said he understood the remark as an acknowledgement the QBCC was being drawn into – or “weaponised” in – an industrial dispute. Former Queensland Building and Construction Commission licensing director Ian Grant giving evidence on Thursday, Commission of Inquiry According to Grant, Bassett told him he was pressured from “the very top” to impose a special licence condition forcing Watpac to engage an independent assessor to audit whether all of its subcontractors were appropriately licensed. Grant said he understood “the very top” to mean de Brenni. Grant said he opposed licence conditions on Watpac because the statutory threshold had not been met and told Bassett he could exercise the power himself.

Advertisement

Instead, Grant said, Bassett declined to make the decision personally, saying it “wouldn’t look right” and whoever signed off on it would need “top cover” because “it’s going to blow up”. “It felt like he was giving assurance that he was going to give me top cover, but I was not buying it,” Grant said. While the QBCC fined PJ Walsh $2611 for earlier unlicensed concreting work – a charge director Patrick Walsh rejected after being told twice by the regulator that his builder’s licence covered the work – no regulatory action was taken against Watpac. Later, Walsh told the inquiry he initially did not intend to tender for a stadium contract, as it would have been a union job. “Everyone’s aware in the industry of the fear and intimidation the CFMEU can do to people,” he said.

Advertisement

But tender they did after a Watpac representative assured him it was not a union job, and Walsh said they came to regret it – a campaign of union harassment was to come his way. Related Article Graphic content

CFMEU Secret witness tells inquiry about drug-fuelled sex party on Gold Coast Walsh’s company already had an enterprise agreement with its workers, he said, to which the CFMEU was not a party and had signed a variation under the state government’s Best Practice Principles policy to pay higher state-funded rates without signing a union EBA. “My employees were egged on to put pressure on me to pay them the uplifted wages, or sign the CFMEU EBA agreement,” he said. In July 2020, the Federal Court found the CFMEU and organiser Grant Harradine had organised an illegal four-day walkout by Walsh’s workers in March 2019 to coerce him into signing a union agreement, imposing civil penalties.

Advertisement

In his witness statement, Walsh said the union’s complaint over his concreting licence came less than two weeks after he obtained a Fair Work Commission order halting the strike, leaving him feeling the QBCC was “doing the CFMEU’s bidding” while senior union official Jade Ingham sat on its board. Walsh said the situation deteriorated to the point where he feared for his safety. “One afternoon a private number came up on my phone and I answered it,” he said. “He said he was a detective … and that on a phone-tap they picked up that a hit was being organised on me, and that I should be vigilant about that. “I asked them what they were going to do about it, and they said that they were going to do nothing because they were working a drug case that was unrelated.”

Advertisement

Commissioner Stuart Wood asked how Walsh could try to remain vigilant about a potential hit. Related Article CFMEU Local businesses sidelined by CFMEU demands on major projects “Drink more and try to forget about it and pretend it wasn’t happening, but that only leads to one place,” Walsh replied. Walsh said he has since stayed away from government-funded jobs through fear of union involvement. Grant also told the inquiry a formal QBCC risk-register entry warning of “regulatory capture” was stripped out in 2018 shortly after since-removed CFMEU Queensland assistant secretary Ingham and National Fire Industry Association president Andrew Hickman were appointed to the expanded board.

Advertisement

Grant said Halton summoned him to his office, said the entry was “inappropriate because of the current composition of the board”, ordered it be removed and instructed him to ensure the words “regulatory capture” no longer be used in general communications. There was also a push to strip builders of their licences on fit-and-proper-person grounds over multiple minor workplace safety improvement notices, Grant said – a move he and assistant commissioner Kate Raymond warned was legally unworkable and would have given the union “incredible leverage” to force directors off company boards. Grant resigned in July 2021 after, he said, he was told he and Raymond were on a “hit list” of executives to be removed before Bassett left office and felt senior leadership had betrayed frontline staff. Major travel agency Flight Centre has warned the accommodation booking system it uses has been affected by “unusual” cyber activity involving a large number of customer records and “limited passport details”. Brisbane-based Flight Centre said while investigations remain ongoing, it believes “that a significant number of customer records in the impacted system may have been accessed by unknown persons”. Flight Centre has disclosed an incident affecting its third-party hotel booking platform. Eamon Gallagher The company said it remained unclear “how many of those records have actually been extracted” from the third-party booking system Flight Centre uses, but most of the accessed records include “only customer names”, some with basic travel information. “A very small percentage is believed to include data such as limited passport details, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, or in rare cases health or mobility information,” Flight Centre said in a statement to the ASX, without naming the accommodation booking provider.

Advertisement

The incident appears to affect the accommodation system used by Flight Centre and travel brands Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent agents. To date, Flight Centre said no customer credit cards, payments or bank account details have been identified as accessed, and flight bookings have not been affected either. Related Article Updated

Aviation Virgin in talks with Boeing, Airbus as it looks to order more planes Flight Centre said it was working with its cybersecurity partner Mandiant “to understand the nature and extent of the activity and to implement appropriate safeguards and containment action”. With Google-subsidiary, Mandiant, the company is working to “contain the activity, change authentication keys and credentials”, it said. Mandiant and Flight Centre have also increased the monitoring on the system. Flight Centre did not say how many customers were affected, when the activity was detected or whether any of the data had surfaced online. The company was contacted for further comment.

Advertisement

Its shares fell about 2 per cent on Thursday. David Hayes, regional vice-president for Asia Pacific and Japan at cybersecurity company Arctic Wolf, said the involvement of an outside booking platform showed some of a company’s biggest vulnerabilities “may lie outside of its own four walls”. “From an attacker’s perspective, why target businesses individually when compromising a single technology provider could potentially expose the customer data of multiple organisations,” he said. The use of third-party contractors in the travel sector has exposed travel-related companies to cyber incidents before. Last year, hackers accessed 5.7 million Qantas customers records through a Philippines call centre contracted by the airlines. The data then included information on frequent flyer accounts, addresses and even the food preferences of thousands of travellers.

Advertisement

The incident saw detailed loyalty program data, including membership in Qantas’ exclusive Chairman’s Lounge, purloined by hacking group Scattered Spider. Qantas customers were caught up again last month after Spanish travel technology provider Amadeus, whose booking systems are used by hotels, travel companies and more than 400 airlines, told affected carriers in late October it had suffered a breach. In April, Booking.com warned customers that unauthorised parties had accessed reservation details including names, email addresses and phone numbers. Samuel Spencer, an adjunct professor of data governance at the University of Canberra, said Flight Centre was the latest travel business hit through its supply chain. “The rise of software as a service provides business with the opportunity to bring new capabilities in quickly, but at the end of the day, it’s their name that customers see,” he said. Spencer said companies needed vendors to spell out who could access their data and where it was stored. “Anyone who can’t answer that and put it in a contract shouldn’t be trusted for sensitive information,” he said.

It is not Flight Centre’s first privacy lapse. In 2017, the company gave participants in a “design jam” event a data file containing more than 6 million customer records, some with passport details that consultants had typed into a free-text field. The incident raises concerns about passport details and travel records being accessed.

Travel giant Flight Centre is investigating a data breach at one of its booking providers which may have exposed customer passport information.

In brief Labor had convinced the Coalition to strike a deal on its domestic gas reservation scheme.

It is hoped the scheme will deliver a "modest oversupply" of gas from 2028.

The Coalition agreed to pass Labor's domestic gas reservation scheme, despite concerns, on Thursday afternoon.

The policy forces liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their supply for the Australian market, starting in 2028.

The Australian Energy Regulator will forecast domestic demand, add a 10 per cent market oversupply buffer, subtract non-exporter supply, and spread the remaining amount across LNG exporters.

title: 'The costs are enormous': Behind some Australians' front doors is a $3.8 billion burden
text:
In brief A new report has described Australia's housing crunch as a public health crisis.

The report's authors say improving housing quality could save the country money and improve Australians' quality of life.

When housing and public health researcher Rebecca Bentley asks a room full of people if they've ever lived in a home with mould, she tends to get a similar response: most raise their hands.

"We do actually have a high tolerance for mould and damp in Australian homes because it's something we've grown to accept a bit," the University of Melbourne professor told SBS News.

But experts say that tolerance comes at a cost.

New research led by the university's Healthy Housing Unit estimates that eliminating household mould could save Australia $3.8 billion in healthcare expenditure and prevent $5.9 billion in lost income over the next 20 years.

And mould isn't the only hazard that could be harming Australians inside their own homes.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The research estimates that 2.5 million Australian households live in unhealthy homes, with issues such as poor ventilation, exposure to pollutants and toxins, pests and extreme indoor temperatures posing risks to occupants' health.

Its authors say high housing prices are pushing Australians into homes that don't meet their needs, with renters more likely to be exposed to poor-quality homes.

"We know that there's an affordability crisis in Australia. That housing supply is low. Rental affordability is not good in Australia at the moment," said Bentley, who is also director of the Centre of Research Excellence in Healthy Housing.

"So all of these things contribute to this large burden of what we would describe as unhealthy housing in Australia."

How can unhealthy housing affect people?

Poor housing conditions can contribute to respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses and poor mental health, as well as affect children's development, productivity and life expectancy.

Bentley said the health consequences of household mould extend beyond physical conditions such as asthma, with exposure also taking a toll on people's mental health — something that was not factored into the modelling.

"So in fact, this estimate of $3.8 billion is actually a relatively conservative estimate," she said.

Distinguished professor Brian Oliver, who researches environmental health at the University of Technology Sydney, said the economic burden of household mould alone might surprise people.

"Even minor ailments cost money.

"It's not like if you've got mould in your bathroom, you're going to drop dead. But if you feel unwell, if you've got days off work, if you're visiting a healthcare practitioner, and if you've got chronic exposure and it leads to chronic disease, then the costs are enormous."

Some housing-related hazards are less visible, such as exposure to excessive noise.

Oliver said noise from busy roads or nearby industrial activity can disrupt residents' sleep, with long-term sleep deprivation linked to a range of health problems.

Living near busy roads can also affect the quality of the air residents breathe.

"Some people live next to busy roads, and they may as well be camping on the road because of the way that their houses work," Oliver told SBS News.

Recognising when your home is making you sick

Oliver said one potential indication that a person's home is affecting their health is if their symptoms improve when they spend time away from it.

He said it's also worth paying attention if a guest observes something about your home that you may have grown accustomed to.

"If you have someone come into your house, and they say, 'Oh, there's an unusual smell', or 'I don't feel so well', that's something you should definitely take notice of."

However, Oliver cautioned against becoming overly concerned about minor exposure to household hazards, noting that the level of exposure matters.

He said there are simple steps people can take to improve the health of their homes, such as opening a bathroom window or switching on an extractor fan after showering to reduce moisture build-up.

If you suspect your home is affecting your health, Oliver recommends speaking to a GP.

What can be done about unhealthy housing?

The report's authors say improving housing quality could save the country money and improve Australians' quality of life.

In particular, the report calls for stronger and more consistent protections for renters nationally, including minimum housing standards covering ventilation, indoor temperatures, repairs, mould and damp.

Roughly a third of the Australian population is renting, and that share is expected to expand over time.

"If renters don't feel like they will be evicted or their rent will be put up if they say ask for mould to be fixed in their home, that's another way in which we can just increase the probability that these problems will be addressed and reduced for people," Bentley said.

The report also calls for stronger construction regulations to improve the quality of new homes, including measures to reduce exposure to environmental noise and extreme indoor temperatures and minimise maintenance issues.

"The choice before us is clear. We can continue to meet the costs of unhealthy housing through hospitals, welfare systems, lost productivity and preventable suffering," Bentley said.

"Or we can invest upstream — in homes that keep people healthy, safe and secure."

title: One of Australia's most popular island escapes is running short of water
text:
IN BRIEF Fiji has declared a national state of disaster due to El Niño-induced water shortages.

Ninety-two communities across Fiji have no water supply, while 372 are at critical water levels.

Australian tourists holidaying in Fiji are being advised to take safety precautions over water, as thousands of locals in surrounding communities struggle to access reliable drinking water, with visitor numbers potentially straining resources further.

Fiji has declared a national state of disaster after an El Niño-driven drought caused widespread water shortages.

Almost 100 communities are now without water, while hundreds more are experiencing critically low supplies, according to the country's National Disaster controller Mitieli Cama.

In addition, Cama says 61 per cent of monitored water sources have reached critical levels.

Fiji has declared a national state of disaster in response to prolonged dry weather and worsening water shortages linked to El Niño conditions. Source: SIPA USA / Sang Qinlong

Fiji's government says the conditions are likely to persist to the middle of next year.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka declared the state of disaster for one month to support "an intensified national response".

He urged people to conserve water, avoid unnecessary burning, and asked businesses to support the federal response.

"We cannot control the climate, but we can act early, use our resources responsibly and stand together through its impacts," he said in a national address last week.

The Fiji Sun reported that government agencies and partners were moving to restore water supplies to affected communities by accelerating emergency water carting, activating boreholes and using water treatment initiatives and alternative water sources.

READ MORE BoM issues a fresh 'super' El Niño reality check for Australia

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade issued new travel advice to Australians on Wednesday, saying tourists should exercise normal safety precautions.

"Water supplies may be impacted, and water rationing may be in place," a Smartraveller post said.

"Extended periods of dry weather may also affect food security and public health.

"Monitor weather conditions before you travel. Check with your travel provider or hotel for updates. Get travel insurance before you go and make sure you’re covered for the duration of your trip."

Fiji's National Disaster Risk Management Office has been helping supply water to communities. Credit: Fiji National Disaster Risk Management Office

But there are concerns growing tourism numbers may put further pressure on water and electricity supplies. Local media reports Fiji's hydroelectric dams could be shut down by the end of January 2027 if the dry conditions persist. It could force the country into expensive fuel-powered generation.

The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association has told the Fiji Sun that visitor numbers could strain resources.

"Fiji’s tourism sector continues to record strong visitor numbers, but that growth also brings increasing demand on essential infrastructure," chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said.

"With approximately 800 additional rooms expected to come online next year, the demands on water and electricity supply will only increase."

In Papua New Guinea, around 680,000 people are expected to receive drought assistance from governmental and UN agencies, as extreme weather and water shortages put communities at risk.

The UN says El Niño is expected to peak in December, naming Papua New Guinea and Tonga as countries most at risk in the region, alongside Myanmar, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, causing weather extremes around the world, including drought in some regions and flooding in others. Some scientists say global warming may increase its intensity.

The US Climate Prediction Center said last week that El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 79 per cent chance of a strong-to-very-strong event through January to March. Australia said in June that El Niño could intensify in the second half of 2026 to become one of the strongest in seven decades.

Fiji's national weather bureau warned in October that strong El Niño conditions persist across the tropical Pacific.

Rainfall is likely to remain below normal from November through April, while daytime temperatures are expected to exceed normal levels through January across most of the country, the Fiji Meteorological Service said.

title: One Nation defector Leah Blyth accuses Liberals of infighting and lack of conviction
text:
In brief Leah Blyth criticised both the Coalition and Labor, saying One Nation would fight for the future of the country.

Her move marks the second defection by a Coalition member, after Barnaby Joyce joined One Nation last year.

South Australian senator Leah Blyth has taken aim at the Liberal Party while exiting the party, accusing it of abandoning its values and declaring One Nation the only party with the conviction to turn Australia "in the right direction".

Blyth, appointed to the Senate in February 2025 to replace retiring senator Simon Birmingham, became One Nation's fifth senator and the first from South Australia after she defected from the Liberals on Wednesday.

Flanked by her new One Nation colleagues at Parliament House on Thursday morning, Blyth said she had done her best to unite the Liberal Party as SA branch president.

But she said the party was plagued by "infighting" and that she did not feel safe, pointing out that she had hired private security to attend the SA branch's recent annual general meeting.

"I believe that One Nation is the only party that has the track record, the consistency, the courage, and the conviction to do what is right to get Australia heading in the right direction," she said.

"I no longer believed that the Liberal Party was the vehicle that was going to bring about the change that our country so desperately needs."

Blyth said the decision to quit was "mine alone" and she had not consulted her Liberal Party colleagues.

She took issue with the party over what she perceived as inconsistent policies, citing its pledge to abandon net zero while remaining in the Paris Agreement.

"My values have been constant and they have been consistent," she said.

"What has changed is the Liberal Party. They have abandoned their values, and so for me, I feel as though the Liberal Party left me, not the other way around."

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said Blyth was a "true conservative".

"This is a win for Australians, people that are fed up with the major political parties who have not listened to them and have not delivered for them," she said.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, who defected from the Nationals nearly a year ago, said Blyth's defection was a "great endorsement of how One Nation is going".

One Nation becoming 'turncoat town'

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume told reporters it was a "disappointing decision".

"The fact that she feels that the Liberal Party doesn't reflect her views anymore is a surprise to all of us. It's certainly not something that she ever mentioned in the party room. But she wasn't a big contributor to the party room," she said.

"I don't think it’s internal division. This is Leah's decision. She believes that she can make her contribution elsewhere. I think that the contribution can be made best by the Liberal Party.

"I think the highlight of this year has been seeing the fact that our team has really united, has gathered around, put its policy agenda out there."

Nationals leader Matt Canavan told reporters on Thursday the defection "smacks of self-interest" and One Nation was becoming "turncoat town".

"It's always disappointing to see someone leave a party that they were elected by," he said.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Leah Blyth's defection "smacked of self-interest". Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

"I think people see that as a defection, as a turncoat. And One Nation is becoming turncoat town right now, where they seem to be much more focused on taking people away from other political parties than changing the government and therefore changing the policy and changing the direction of this country."

He said he didn't buy Blyth's explanation that she joined One Nation due to its policies.

"It instead just smacks of self-interest; [she] went to the election last year supporting net zero," he said.

title: Donald Trump announces new tariffs on China, Japan and the EU
text:
In brief A previous tariff regime under national emergency laws was struck down by the US Supreme Court in February.

The new tariffs rely on a different court-tested trade law, with maximum rates of 20 to 40 per cent.

United States President Donald Trump has announced new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.

Australia was not among the countries affected.

His administration proposed new maximum potential rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent to counter excess industrial capacity that it says these countries are promoting.

But the US Trade Representative's (USTR) office said it intends to cap new tariffs at lower levels agreed under trade deals that are completed or still under negotiation.

In unveiling the results of an eight-month investigation into unfair trade practices related to excess industrial capacity, USTR aims to further rebuild Trump's tariff leverage after the Supreme Court, in February, struck down his broad global duties under a national emergencies law.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The effort also seeks to put Trump's tariffs and associated trade agreements on firmer legal and political grounds by backing them with a court-tested trade law, and by addressing foreign subsidies and industrial policies that are viewed as major trade problems by both Republicans and Democrats.

Separately, USTR proposed a new 10 per cent tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and an increase in duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brazil to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.

The products were previously exempt from Trump's 25 per cent tariffs on Brazilian goods, imposed in July as part of a separate investigation.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer said he decided to propose the tariff increases after months of talks between the US and Brazil made "no meaningful progress".

China tops excess capacity rates

Under the excess factory capacity inquiry, USTR said China would face the highest capped rate of 20 per cent, added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on 10 January. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40 per cent, the USTR said.

Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with the US, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail.

Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a 25 January public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base.

The duties would not stack on top of prior tariffs of 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent imposed under a separate US probe into lax enforcement of anti-forced labour laws in 60 economies, nor would they add to national security duties on steel, aluminium, autos and other goods.

Greer said the proposed tariffs also would not apply to about US $30 billion ($45 billion) of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

The US has long accused China of subsidising industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.

A spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China is a source of excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"The so-called issue of 'industrial overcapacity' does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation," the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Lower rates for trade deals

The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18 per cent for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15 per cent, including existing "Most Favoured Nation" duties, for Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the EU and Switzerland.

India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail, the USTR said.

Singapore would receive a capped tariff rate of 10 per cent.

Greer told CNBC the proposed caps were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year that also lowered barriers to US exports.

"We're sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said, adding that the capped rates are no surprise to trading partners.

Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain underway, Greer said.

Trump's tariffs and their impact on rising living costs were a major issue in Democrats' sweeping victory in midterm elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans' midterm losses found 62 per cent of respondents supported efforts by Democrats to repeal them.

title: 'Incompetent': Bereaved parents lash Angus Taylor after generic email blunder
text:
In Brief Bereaved mothers say they felt "gaslit" after seeking support for stronger social media age limits.

Angus Taylor's office has not acknowledged the error, despite being alerted nearly two weeks ago.

This story contains references to suicide

Two bereaved families who advocate for children's online safety say they were "gaslit" by Opposition leader Angus Taylor after they spoke to him to seek support for stronger social media age limits, criticising his response as "incompetent" after receiving a delayed email referring to a different bill.

Online safety campaigners Mia Bannister and Emma Mason, who both had children that died following severe online harm, said they followed up their September meeting with Taylor with a passionate email asking for action. But his office's response three weeks later included a word-for-word copy of the Liberal Party’s website page about a different piece of legislation, they told SBS News.

Taylor's office then failed to acknowledge the mistake when SBS News highlighted the error 13 days ago and has not contacted the parents.

Bannister founded Ollie's Echo, a charity devoted to the memory of her son Ollie, who died by suicide in January 2024 aged 14 following sustained online bullying and a short battle with anorexia. She advocates against bullying, body image pressures, eating disorders, and online harms through school and community programs.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

She and Mason met with Taylor's office on 8 September about why he should back changes to the social media minimum age bill.

The parents say they thought Taylor had listened, but his response indicated otherwise.

Two days later, Taylor voted against the changes to the social media minimum age bill, leaving the parents who met with him greatly disappointed and accusing him of politicising young people who have been harmed.

They sent him an email asking why he had voted against the changes and three weeks later, received an email stating the Coalition was opposed to the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 — a different bill to the one they had discussed with him. The email contained the same wording as the Liberal Party's website, on why the party would not support the digital duty of care bill, which passed the parliament on Wednesday, after Labor struck a deal with the Greens.

Communications Minister Anika Wells with bereaved parents Mia Bannister, Robb Evans, Emma Mason at Parliament House in July. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Bannister told SBS News she was "gobsmacked" that Taylor's email didn't address the issues they talked about during the meeting.

"At least [former Liberal leader] Peter Dutton showed some empathy when I met him," Bannister said. "Not once in this whole process has the Opposition reached out except for [Queensland MP] Andrew Wallace."

"Yes, we were in Canberra for the exposure draft for the digital duty of care. However, when we sat down with the leader of the Opposition and Andrew Wallace, we did not discuss the digital duty of care. We discussed the fact that they voted against the amendments to the social media minimum age legislation," Bannister said.

She said she felt Taylor was deliberately trying to lump the digital duty of care bill into his response because the Coalition did not support it.

"I hate these terms of gaslighting and ghosting ... [but] absolutely, it would be gaslighting us completely."

When Bannister gave evidence at the Digital Duty of Care Senate hearing earlier this month, Communication Minister Anika Wells' office "picked up the phone and thanked us again".

"I don't think the Coalition realise the toll it takes on us every time we have to get up and speak about our kids, but we do it because we feel if we stop, there's no one else driving it forward. So that's why we do what we do.

"I just found the leader of the Opposition very cold, whereas we've had very different experiences with other members of parliament. It was the Coalition that pushed for the social media laws in the first place, and then Labor took it on. So I find it actually extremely rude, and yes, incompetent."

Mason told SBS News it was "concerning" that the Coalition, which got the issue of child protection onto the national stage, "now decided that because of whatever's going on in their own political sphere, they need to do some point scoring".

"I spoke to [former Liberal leader] Sussan Ley, just before she resigned [in February this year] and we talked openly about the situation, and then there's just been crickets," Mason said.

"So it's very odd. And then, having actually reached out, [Taylor] writes an email that doesn't address what we were addressing; we correct that, and then again, no answer. I think intrinsically he's a good man. It's not malicious, but it's just odd."

Mason began campaigning for online safety after her 15-year-old daughter, Tilly Rosewarne, died by suicide in February 2022 following severe cyberbullying. Mason spoke at the United Nations in September 2025 urging global leaders to raise social media age limits and continues to push for safety online.

Taylor's office has been known to have communications mishaps in the past, including the 2019 "Fantastic. Great move. Well done Angus." social media blunder where he or someone in his office was found to be commenting on his Facebook posts and the controversy over incorrect travel figures used to attack Sydney lord mayor Clover Moore, which he blamed on his office.

A spokesperson for Taylor told SBS News their "hearts go out to every family who has lost a child", and they "strongly support laws that keep children safe online".

"That is why the Coalition led the way on the original social media minimum age legislation, which passed Parliament with bipartisan support," the spokesperson said.

"We want to see children better protected online. We consider that the best way to achieve this is through proper implementation of the social media ban, which, disappointingly, has, to date, only seen around a 5 per cent reduction in teens on social media.

"Mr Taylor held a constructive meeting on the legislation. The Coalition moved amendments to the Bill to address privacy concerns and strengthen safety, which the Government ultimately rejected.

"Our office will be in touch with Emma and Mia to fully outline the Coalition’s position on the Bill."

Bannister and Mason shared with SBS News the email chain to Taylor's office following the meeting. They expressed anger and disappointment and urged that they not be treated as "political props".

"We repeatedly pleaded with you to put politics aside and we meant it," their email read in part.

"We had hoped that was something we could count on both sides of Parliament to fight for with us. We remain profoundly disappointed that this was not the case."
