title: Higher taxes on trusts set to become law after Labor secures Greens support
text:
In brief New laws will impose a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts.

Private jet owners will have to pay the same fuel excise rate as motorists under the new laws.

Individuals and small businesses will have to pay higher taxes on trusts after the Greens gave the proposal the support it needs to pass the Senate.

The law, announced in the government's May budget, will impose a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts, but will now also hit private jet owners with a higher fuel levy, as the minor party demanded.

Discretionary trusts can be used to split income, including among relatives and families running businesses — something critics argue is a way for the wealthy to dodge higher income taxes.

"Discretionary trusts are basically a legalised defrauding of the Commonwealth that is overwhelmingly exploited by super wealthy people to avoid paying their fair share," Greens treasury spokesperson Nick McKim told reporters on Wednesday.

"At the end of the day, today Australia's tax system will just be a little bit fairer, and it will be fairer because we are cracking down on the 1 per cent."

title: Australia's inflation problem is growing again. When can we expect relief?
text:
In brief The consumer price index has risen to its highest level in three years.

It comes after grim unemployment figures were released last week.

Australia's inflation numbers are heading in the wrong direction, with a shocking rise in the price of goods and services leaving the prospect of a rate cut further away.

The headline consumer price index (CPI) rose 4.9 per cent in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 4.3 per cent in the 12 months to September. It's now at its highest in three years.

It wasn't the news many Australians seeking relief after a wave of painful rate hikes this year were expecting.

The figures — including the underlying rate — even floored markets and economists who, while bracing for inflation to rise this month, did not expect it to be this high.

"This is a very serious moment for our economy, and we will respond in substantial ways," Treasurer Jim Chalmers said, reacting to the data.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Why did inflation increase in October?

Transport costs, electricity fees, and construction of new builds were the main factors behind the surge. The rise in electricity prices was due to government rebates ending, increasing the hit to consumers' pockets.

Fuel prices rose 6.3 per cent in October — averaging 246.7 cents per litre for petrol nationally — and were a major contributor to the inflation spike.

Headline inflation has hit a three-year high. Source: SBS News

It was above expectations.

Bendigo Bank chief economist David Robertson said while the headline 4.9 per cent was close to forecasts, the core rate of inflation at 3.8 per cent was above consensus.

"It is also above the [Reserve Bank's] latest forecasts, which expected core inflation to remain steady at 3.6 per cent," he said in a statement.

How is the economy faring?

There were already concerns that Australia could be heading for a recession, if not technically in one already, after grim unemployment figures were released last week.

The jobless rate is now at its highest level in five years, and is predicted to increase.

Macquarie Bank has now joined HSBC in forecasting a 50-50 chance of a recession.

Cherelle Murphy, EY's chief economist for Oceania, says it's not often that both unemployment and inflation rise.

"It's often that we get one or not the other. What we're sort of seeing at the moment is an economy which is definitely slowing down," she told ABC News.

The figures will leave the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) pondering whether the steep rise in the unemployment rate is enough — or whether the shock inflation figures will push it towards another rate hike.

"It's going to continue to grow up faster than expected, and so then the RBA is going to increasingly have to make a decision between whether they're going to set interest rates to light inflation or whether they're going to take jobs," University of Sydney economist Gareth Bryant told SBS News.

Could 2027 bring some relief??

Chalmers said despite the inflation surprise, CPI is still expected to come down to the target band in mid next year, and the economy will continue to grow.

But there will still be some painful months ahead.

"When it comes to the way that we see the year ahead, 2026 has been an especially difficult year for people. We expect this inflation for a range of reasons to hang around for a bit longer than anyone would like," he said.

The RBA's rate hikes are still filtering through the economy — so the inflation figures paint the current picture, not the future.

"This is kind of looking at the 2026 economy — it doesn't necessarily tell us what's going to go on in 2027," Murphy said.

"So yes, we will see the economy slow. Yes, we'll probably see unemployment hover around these levels and maybe even move a little higher.

"But it's what happens to inflation throughout the course of next year that matters. And as long as the Reserve Bank sees it start to come down, it's probably going to be fairly satisfied that it's done enough. If it continues to surprise on the upside because something else changed or that inflationary pressure simply isn't going away, then that's when they'll be thinking about further rate hikes."

READ MORE The money changes you can make, as Australians told to expect financial pain

Robertson anticipates the cash rate will remain unchanged when the RBA meets next month.

"I expect the official cash rate will remain steady at 4.85 per cent for most of 2027, and still expect there will likely be a longer, more drawn-out cash rate cycle than consensus," he said in a statement.

"Labour markets continue to suggest there's no need for further rate hikes. Volatile global markets are complicating the outlook again, suggesting that current rates are sufficiently restrictive."

But a rate cut by mid-2027 is now more unlikely.

"With employment softening, housing under pressure and financial conditions restrictive, we believe the bar for another hike remains high, even after this upside surprise," said Joseph Marassa, strategist at exchange-traded fund provider Global X ETFs in a statement.

"However, until price pressures are convincingly contained, rate relief may remain a distant prospect."

title: Jensen Huang’s mega-status as the world’s ‘AI bank’ raises Trump concerns
text:
In brief Jensen Huang apologised to staff as he returned to Nvidia following a scandal involving multiple affairs.

An initial market rally faded as scrutiny of the AI giant's relationship to US President Donald Trump persisted.

Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff and said he was in therapy on Tuesday, as a stock rally triggered by his shock return as CEO faltered amid persistent doubts over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.

Huang resigned on 12 November over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman some US intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese spy. His departure sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to AI tumbling.

However, after initially saying it did not intend to reinstate Huang, Nvidia's board announced the company's founder was "the right person to lead Nvidia" and his reinstatement served stockholders, employees, partners and customers.

"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang told an hour-long all-hands meeting at the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, the New York Times reported after reviewing a livestream of the event.

He told staff it was "not acceptable" that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he was back because United States President Donald Trump had pressured the board.

But Trump told CNBC on Tuesday that he had been in contact with directors about Huang's return.

"I spoke to them, let me put it that way," Trump said. "And I convinced them."

After vaulting more than 30 per cent on Tuesday, Nvidia shares were down about 6 per cent at close.

"The optimism faded quickly" for Nvidia, wrote analyst Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with "questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering".

So far, Tuesday's surge had been a "one-day wonder", according to Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of investment firm Mahoney Asset Management.

"We are not seeing an upside follow-through today at all."

Trump pressure

Trump's push for Huang's reinstatement was an intervention in the business world like no US president has done before.

"There's no precedent for any of this," Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.

According to media reports, the 80-year-old billionaire invited himself onto a conference call of Nvidia's board to plead the case of the chip giant's founder.

READ MORE Donald Trump hails Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang after affair scandal

Trump assured board members that Huang would face no action from the US justice department — a promise he could make, as the department is headed by his former personal lawyer.

Trump also intervened in the Nvidia affair to halt a plunge in artificial intelligence stocks triggered by Huang's resignation, which had raised fears of a broader stock market correction.

Trump was reportedly talked into backing the return of the Taiwan-born CEO after top tech investors told him the US economy and Wall Street depended on it.

The unprecedented move breaks with the long-held US tradition of free enterprise, which rejects government intervention outright — or at least overly explicit state direction of the economy.

At the height of the financial crisis in 2009, the White House secured the departure of the head of General Motors, a carmaker then being kept afloat by government aid, but then-president Barack Obama did not boast about it.

The Nvidia case is very different.

For one thing, the US government has no financial ties to the thriving company.

Trump, however, is an investor in Nvidia, owning as many as 370,000 shares as of 30 September, according to filings.

Shares linked to the AI boom have fallen steeply in recent weeks amid fears that the AI bubble, inflated since the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT in 2022, was finally bursting.

In downward-trending markets, quick rebounds are common but "tend to get negated and that has been the sequence since early October", Mahoney said, adding that "sellers have absolute control of the market here".

Nvidia is central to the AI investment story — its powerful processors are the key tool for training and running the AI models believed to be at the heart of a technological revolution.

The massive spending on its AI chips and software, housed in sprawling data centres, catapulted the company into the ranks of the world's most valuable firms.

Huang used that success to turn Nvidia into a kind of central bank for other AI companies and startups, doling out loans and financial guarantees to firms that would otherwise struggle to borrow from traditional lenders.

"Jensen out of Nvidia basically was the equivalent of the [US Federal Reserve] raising rates by 50 bits," Dan Ives, technology analyst at merchant bank Yorkville Ives, told SBS' On the Money podcast.

"I mean, he was that important. And I think, [in relation to] the circular financing, he's essential. He is the AI bank."

'Good corporate citizen'

Investors are also weighing a barrage of legal challenges facing Huang and Nvidia.

The board that let Huang go and then rehired him is still overseeing an internal investigation into concerns that he may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, even though Trump says he has been cleared.

The US justice department is separately investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that allegedly bought Nvidia processors and routed them to Chinese customers in violation of US export restrictions. One of the women Huang had an affair with, Alice Huang (no relation), was an executive at Megaspeed, but stepped down from the role in 2025.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has also reportedly opened an inquiry into Nvidia's accounting practices and potentially misleading communication to shareholders.

"Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That shouldn't be groundbreaking," US attorney-general Todd Blanche told reporters at an unrelated press conference.

"If Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people," he added.

Jensen Huang will nevertheless face lawmakers at a closed-door hearing before three House committees on 1 December and a livestreamed Senate committee hearing on 3 December.

"There's gonna be more scrutiny about China and the loophole revenue, but let's just be clear. Jensen is like the pilot on the aeroplane. You don't want the pilot on an aeroplane taking a parachute out mid-flight when you're going into a thunderstorm," Ives said.

Politicians from both parties have expressed anger over the circumstances of Huang's return, and the scrutiny is likely to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

title: US officials defend plan to destroy unstable explosives in Iowa after Trump pause
text:
In brief Residents near a small Iowa town have been urged to evacuate before the planned destruction of unstable explosives.

The operation has raised concerns about potential lead contamination and public safety.

The United States Army has urged residents of a small Iowa town and nearby areas to evacuate ahead of the planned detonation of some 4,500kg of unstable and degraded explosive material.

The plan — which has sparked fears of lead contamination — is to destroy the country's entire stockpile of lead azide, a material previously used to trigger other explosives in munitions but which officials say is now at risk of spontaneous detonation. The detonation is set for Thursday.

The US Federal Emergency Management Agency is "supporting the recommended relocation for all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas" out of "an abundance of caution", the army said in a public safety advisory. Middletown has a population of around 360.

The destruction of the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant had been scheduled for 20 November.

But it was postponed by three days, after which US President Donald Trump ordered a pause in the detonation, which is now scheduled to proceed.

"There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide ... is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation," acting army secretary Adam Telle told a news conference on Wednesday.

On Tuesday, Trump ordered a pause on the planned detonation, saying it would proceed only if an appeals court signed off and if Iowa's incoming governor, Democrat Rob Sand, agreed to let it go ahead.

title: The money changes you can make, as Australians told to expect financial pain
text:
in brief Jim Chalmers has warned Australians to brace for stubborn inflation and sustained economic pain in 2027.

Financial experts say auditing recurring household bills and building emergency buffers are among the steps people can take.

With Australians being warned that more economic pain is on the horizon, financial experts are urging households to future-proof their finances before the end of the year.

On Monday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers warned in a rare parliamentary statement that the Australian economy is at a "serious" moment and that serious decisions must be made in response.

"Global and domestic factors, including the ongoing effect of higher interest rates, mean our economy and our people will be under more pressure for longer than we would like," Chalmers told parliament.

"We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier."

The ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine, rising fuel costs, and debt from the COVID-19 pandemic are all contributing factors to a looming 2027 which the treasurer said will see unemployment and inflation remain high while growth slows.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Still, he added, wages are expected to grow at 3 per cent, while business investment remains double Treasury forecasts.

Opposition Treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said on Tuesday the government was trying to "front run" further bad news ahead of "what is going to be a very challenging year".

With such a gloomy economic outlook, experts say now is the best time to consider personal finances to ensure stability in the year ahead.

"We can't control the larger economy, but we can control ours," Taylor Blackburn, personal finance specialist at Finder, told SBS News.

A two-speed economy?

The latest inflation figures will be released on Wednesday and are expected to show stubbornly high inflation similar to the 4.3 per cent recorded in September. Many households are struggling to keep up with the rising cost of everyday items.

Rising interest rates are also squeezing borrowers, with five interest rate hikes since January.

At the same time, for those with money in the bank and no debt to pay off, higher interest rates mean greater return on savings.

Canstar's Sally Tindall told SBS News that, on paper, Australians look well off, with a record $1.79 trillion in the bank and $8.8 billion in extra mortgage repayments last quarter.

"In reality, Australian households are living two very different financial lives," Tindall said.

"While many are sitting on giant buffers, others are stretched to breaking point, often without a buffer to fall back on."

Commonwealth Bank data has recently shown that 85 per cent of its home loan customers are ahead on their mortgage repayments by an average of 32 months.

However, 15 per cent have nothing extra they could contribute to their payments, while 1 per cent are in arrears.

It's a potentially growing problem, with unemployment hitting 4.9 per cent — its highest in five years — in October. It's expected to breach 5 per cent for the first time since the pandemic.

"While trying to pay the rising cost of everyday expenses such as the mortgage, rent, grocery bills and transport could well get tougher in 2027, imagine trying to achieve this without money coming in," Tindall said.

Audit finances for greater predictability

The number one thing financial experts advise when considering how to stabilise household budgets is to sit down and work out exactly where money is going.

"Take a half day off work," Tindall said. "Write out a list of every single recurring expense, sort them in order of size and start haggling, switching or ditching."

Tindall said cutting back on expenses such as mortgage, groceries, insurances, electricity, gas, mobile, NBN, TV subscriptions and even gym memberships can help you save "today, tomorrow" and across 2027.

Blackburn said, for borrowers, their mortgage loan will likely be their biggest outgoing and should face the brunt of scrutiny.

"If you haven’t checked your home loan rate in the past year, or don’t know what your rate is to start with, you’re probably paying too much," he said.

"Start with a quick phone call. Find a cheaper rate online, ring your lender and ask them to match it.

"If they won't move, it might be time to refinance. Even a small reduction can save you thousands of dollars over the life of your loan."

Getting the mortgage down, Blackburn said, is the best use of any money saved as the faster it is paid off, the more money is saved overall.

Similarly, debt on credit cards or buy now, pay later programs can be shifted to 0 per cent balance-transfer cards to avoid interest charges.

Don't pay the 'loyalty tax'

Sticking with a utility or services provider often provides little benefit, while switching frequently can present opportunities.

"We crunched the numbers on energy, broadband, and mobile costs and found that Australians paid a collective $6.7 billion in loyalty tax last year," Blackburn said. "That's $569 per household."

Adding subscription or bill renewal dates to your calendar, particularly for annual fees, can help avoid getting "stung" when an introductory rate rolls over into a higher price, Blackburn advises.

Canstar research has found that switching or renegotiating five of a household's largest bills can save the typical home as much as $4,000 over 12 months.

Have an emergency buffer

With growing global instability and challenges in the domestic labour market, financial experts say creating and maintaining a financial buffer is a key priority.

"Even setting aside $20 or $50 every time you're paid can take the sting out of a surprise bill," Blackburn said. "Then aim to have at least 3 months' and ideally 6 months' worth of living expenses saved."

"If you do one thing today, audit your emergency buffer," Tindall stressed, adding that households should consider jump-starting their savings with a big financial decision such as selling a second car, postponing a holiday, or taking a second job.

"None are likely to be ideal, but having an emergency parachute is something every household should have," she said.

With high interest rates, Blackburn noted that an emergency fund should be put to work.

"If your ongoing savings account rate doesn't start with at least a '5' you’re missing out on free money," he said.

With Christmas approaching, often a very expensive time of year, Tindall suggests trying to avoid the spending spree if possible.

"Consider flipping the script with a 'nothing new' Christmas," she said.

"You might find that your friends and family thank you for suggesting what they were too worried to suggest themselves."

title: A third-country link allowing Nvidia chips to get to China is under scrutiny
text:
In Brief Singapore says its investigation into Megaspeed is continuing as the US moves to blacklist the AI firm.

Singapore's prime minister says the country won't be used to bypass export controls on advanced AI chips.

Singapore's prime minister says the AI firm at the centre of the Nvidia spy scandal is still being investigated there, as the US government moves to blacklist it over allegations that it moved advanced AI chips to China in breach of American export controls.

Speaking in Canberra on Tuesday, Lawrence Wong rejected suggestions that Singapore had become a weak link in the escalating technology competition between the United States and China, while stressing that his government does not want the city-state used to circumvent US export restrictions.

"We do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America's export controls," Wong said when asked by SBS News about the case.

"What we do is facilitate checks by America to enforce its own laws."

The scandal revolves around an extramarital affair between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, who worked at Megaspeed, the Singaporean company suspected of diverting restricted AI chips to China.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Alice Huang was in contact with an officer at a Chinese intelligence agency from 2025 until late in 2026, The New York Times reported, citing people briefed on US intelligence reports.

Wong said Singapore had investigated Megaspeed and Alice Huang after concerns emerged that advanced AI chips may have been routed through the company to Chinese customers.

"We were thorough with Alice Huang. We took her in, we investigated her, but we eventually released her because there was no basis for further prosecution. America understands what we have done," he said.

Megaspeed investigations ongoing

Wong said investigations into Megaspeed remain active, particularly on the US side, as authorities in both countries exchange information.

"We are continuing to have discussions with American authorities where the end-users are, to confirm the verification of various documents," Wong said.

"These investigations into Megaspeed are ongoing on the American side."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addressed reporters alongside Wong, reiterating his position that the allegations are "serious".

"Is Australia a party to any of these arrangements? Quite clearly not," he said.

"It's a matter for the company, it's a matter for the United States and it's a matter for Singapore."

READ MORE Donald Trump hails Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang after affair scandal

Megaspeed says it's a "legitimate and lawful business" and that Huang left the company in August 2025.

Wong disputed claims that the case showed weaknesses in Singapore's oversight of sensitive technology exports. He said the chips were never intended for use in Singapore and merely passed through the country's commercial networks.

"The chips were routed through Singapore to other countries," he said. "Obviously we cannot investigate all that's happening in these countries."

He added that Singapore has sought more information from US authorities about the ultimate destinations of the chips and is working closely with Washington to help enforce export-control rules.

"We are also looking at companies that may be using Singapore and exploiting Singapore's position to reroute chips through Singapore to other parts of Southeast Asia or to other countries," Wong said.

"We do not have full information on where all these chips are sent to. They are not sent to Singapore as a final destination, but the US has growing interest in this area of chips coming through Singapore and being transited or rerouted."

Megaspeed blacklisted by US authorities

Earlier on Tuesday, the US commerce department announced plans to blacklist Megaspeed and affiliated companies to block them from buying or selling goods in the United States.

US authorities have been investigating the company since at least 2024 over allegations it helped move restricted Nvidia computer chips into China, bypassing export bans imposed by Washington.

China has been restricted from accessing advanced semiconductor technology since 2022 to slow China's development of cutting-edge artificial intelligence systems.

Megaspeed, which operates data centres and cloud computing infrastructure across Southeast Asia, and China both deny the allegations that Alice Huang is linked to Chinese intelligence.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will be questioned in closed-door interviews with US congressional committees examining the scandal.

Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive 11 days after his resignation following consultations with US government officials.

Neither Wong nor Albanese directly addressed questions about Huang's return during the Canberra press conference.

The two leaders signed an agreement to deepen co-operation on AI.

title: Tech giants set to face major fines: How will the updated online safety bill work?
text:
IN BRIEF The Greens have reached an agreement with Labor on passing digital duty of care legislation.

Labor had to make a deal with the Greens after it became clear the Coalition would not support the bill.

Tech giants could be fined billions of dollars and face lawsuits from people harmed by social media algorithms, and a new regulator will offer people a place to appeal, after a deal was made to pass new online safety standards.

Labor's digital duty of care laws will force online services, including social media, online games and AI chatbots, to take reasonable steps to reduce serious online harm.

The reforms will pass the Senate with support from the Greens after the party negotiated concessions from the government on Tuesday.

Labor forfeited ministerial powers to classify new online harms, and carved out small businesses and religious organisations from the bill after a Senate committee suggested changes on Friday.

The Greens, who hold the balance of power in the upper house, forced the government to amend the laws on Tuesday so people can sue tech companies directly for harm caused, and fine platforms up to 5 per cent of global revenue if they fail to shield users from harm caused by addictive algorithms, or fail to take down harmful content.

For Meta, which runs Facebook and Instagram, that could mean fines in the order of $10 billion. Labor's original proposal had set fines at $109 million.

The rate of hateful conduct found on Facebook by users is rising. Source: SBS News

"Like every other company selling products in Australia, big tech will finally be held responsible for the harm that their products cause. Just like food producers and toy manufacturers," Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said.

People will also have the choice to turn algorithms on or off and see the content they want to see, she said.

"It's time to dump the doomscroll. For the first time, tech companies will now have to recognise the addictive nature of their platforms and prevent harm from features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and gamification that keep Australians hooked online for hours longer than they want to be.

"The Greens have also secured the establishment of an independent ombudsman to help Australian consumers manage disputes with tech platforms."

US ambassador hits out at new laws after meeting minister

Communications Minister Anika Wells said she met with US ambassador David Brat on Tuesday as part of ongoing "constructive dialogue" with the US government.

"It has been a long-signalled intent of our government that we would pass these laws because online safety is such a priority for us. I think the ambassador and I had a really constructive meeting, really friendly meeting," Wells said.

"I think we would say there are points of difference, and we are riding them out."

READ MORE A third-country link allowing Nvidia chips to get to China is under scrutiny

Following the meeting with Wells, Brat said: "Free speech is the foundation of a free society, and protecting it is a US priority".

He said he had expressed to Wells the Trump administration's "well-known objections" to the legislation, saying "vaguely defined 'harms', backed by penalties of up to 5 per cent of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech".

"As Australia's largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors."

The US embassy forcefully told the government in September to "withdraw any plans to mandate that platforms algorithmically suppress content based on ambiguous government-defined safety criteria".

What platforms have to do

The laws focus on how digital services are designed and managed, so social media firms will need to assess risks and take action to protect users from harmful or illegal material.

They would also have to protect under-18s from content and features that may be harmful, including pornography, material that encourages eating disorders and features that could cause serious distress.

The bill also gives social media users aged 16 and over a choice to turn off algorithm-recommended feeds and see posts from accounts they follow.

It expands the eSafety Commissioner's powers over apps and websites used to create fake nude images, and shortens the required response time for cyberbullying and abuse complaints from 48 hours to 24.

Professional news and entertainment material are exempt from the new laws.

READ MORE Small businesses spared from online crackdown as crunch time looms for government

A new independent ombudsman will help Australians challenge social media account bans and deal with other issues.

Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) Cynthia Gebert said thousands of Australians seek help from the TIO when they're locked out of social media and email accounts.

"It's great that Australians will soon have access to a free, fair and independent dispute resolution scheme when big tech gets things wrong," Gebert said.

"We look forward to working with the government on the development of the external dispute resolution scheme."

Why is the Coalition against the bill?

The bill makes platforms responsible for foreseeable harms linked to their services and gives people stronger ways to seek redress. The Coalition has opposed the laws, warning freedom of speech may be policed or curtailed.

Opposition communications spokesperson Sarah Henderson told reporters on Monday the laws threaten "not only the free speech of Australians, but also the online safety of Australians".

"It is a blank cheque for political censorship because it allows the regulator to basically prohibit any type of serious harm directed towards children," Henderson said.

"We have very strong current laws under the Online Safety Act, including the 17 codes and standards, and the eSafety Commissioner is using those laws right now to prosecute Telegram for refusing or declining to remove pro-terror material," she said.

There was little hope the Coalition would support the changes, with the Opposition instead calling for a crackdown on harmful content via existing laws.

Her party was particularly concerned the bill would allow government ministers and the eSafety Commissioner to mandate what was harmful.

Henderson said she will push for better parental protections online when parliament returns next year.

Meta declined to comment. SBS News has also asked Google and TikTok for comment.

title: Donald Trump hails Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang after affair scandal

Huang resigned as CEO after his affair with a woman thought to be a Chinese spy was made public.

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and chief executive of Nvidia, just days after his offer to return to the artificial intelligence giant was rejected.

Huang had previously built a reputation as one of the industry's leading evangelists and could call on the support of powerful backers including US President Donald Trump.

The business leader's return was the latest twist in the fallout from Huang's admission of an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chairman Harvey C. Jones said in a statement.

Trump praised Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang.

In a telephone interview with US broadcaster CNBC, Trump suggested the scandal could prove to be "a net positive" by highlighting Nvidia's technological advances.

"I don't think he's going to be diminished at all," he said, predicting Huang would return at "an almost higher level".

Trump said he had intervened in the board's decision.

"I believe my intervention was very important," he said.

Trump said he spoke to Huang and was assured the AI figurehead would work harder than before his fall.

He said the attorney general had confirmed that US authorities possessed no evidence Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct, but urged Nvidia to continue investigating its compliance with restrictions on advanced chip sales to China.

The Justice Department is currently conducting a criminal investigation involving potential export control violations into Megaspeed, the Singapore-based cloud computing firm where Alice Huang, the suspected spy Huang conducted an affair with, was an executive.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House of Representatives speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries vowed sweeping investigations into Nvidia, Trump and his senior officials, with Jeffries singling out commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.

"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump administration for personal financial gain," Jeffries said.

In a statement, Huang said he was "honoured" to return to the company and that he resumes the responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment".

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang's statement said.

Nvidia shares soared 33 per cent to $US165.57 ($250.16) at the opening bell on Monday, moments after Huang's return was announced.

That price was far below the all-time high of $US239.24 ($357.26) the stock reached last month.

Huang's reinstatement comes after days of speculation about whether he would return.

Supporters set up an online petition calling for him to get his job back that drew many signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters, including Elon Musk.

It's not the first time a tech industry leader has been sacked because of transparency concerns and then quickly rehired after an outpouring of support from staff and investors.

Hundreds of home buyers of two major property developments, one each in Dee Why and Blacktown, have been left in limbo as nearly $20 million they paid in deposits has gone missing, and the solicitor at the centre of the fiasco has had his legal licence suspended. Lawyer Ken Neville at Branston Neville Lawyers has been suspended by the Law Society pending court proceedings. Solicitor Ken Mark Neville and his Bella Vista-based law firm Branston Neville Lawyers are being pursued through the Supreme Court by developer Landmark Group amid allegations the home buyer deposits on 285 units remain unaccounted for from the firm’s trust account. Justice Anthony McGrath has ordered an account of the project’s funds by Neville, and for the funds to be transferred to a new trust account. An emergency council meeting of the Law Society of NSW was called late on Thursday afternoon at which Neville’s legal licence was suspended and a manager appointed to take control of the practice with immediate effect.

Advertisement

“As this matter may be the subject of further investigation, and with related matters presently before the court, any further comment at this time would be inappropriate,” a spokesperson for the Law Society said. Of the estimated 285 buyers affected by the missing deposits, about half are in the Dee Why development called Casa Delmar, where buyers were due to settle this week. Among them is Lobsang Thupten, a 48-year-old refugee from Tibet who took the day off work on Thursday to take possession of his newly built first home. Instead, the gyprocker, from TB Yak Plastering, is left wondering what will happen to his deposit on the nearly $1.5 million apartment and when he’ll be able to move in. Lobsang Thupten outside the Dee Why apartment he was due to settle on Thursday. Janie Barrett A spokesperson for Landmark Group said no purchaser had been asked to pay their deposit again, and the solicitors of affected purchasers had been advised. Landmark is yet to confirm the revised settlement date.

Advertisement

According to a source familiar with the operations at Landmark Group, more than $24 million in deposits were held in the trust account of Branston Neville Lawyers from 285 unit sales in the Casa Delmar development at Dee Why and the Second Avenue development at Blacktown. However, when the developer changed law firms a few months ago, only about $5 million of those deposits were transferred to the trust account of their newly appointed law firm Hendrix Legal. The Delmar development at Dee Why. Janie Barrett When the deposits were not transferred, Landmark reported the matter to the Law Society of NSW and commenced proceedings in the Supreme Court. A Landmark spokesperson said freeze orders had been issued against the firm and its principal’s bank accounts. Arash Tavakoli, who heads Landmark Group, issued a statement on Thursday saying he was dismayed by the situation, particularly for first home buyers and families who had planned to move in before Christmas.

Advertisement

“[Buyers] did everything right,” Tavakoli said. “They paid their deposits into a solicitor’s trust account, which should be the safest place their money could be. We are committed to every one of these sales, and we will keep fighting until every deposit is accounted for.” Casa Delmar is a complex of 288 apartments, almost all of which had sold before the project was completed. Of those, about 140 sales are affected by the missing deposit funds. The 21-storey development at Blacktown is almost complete and almost entirely sold. Of its 343 apartments, 145 apartments are affected. Of the 343 apartments in Landmark’s Second Avenue development at Blacktown, about 145 apartments are affected by the missing deposit funds. Lauren Sudol, 28, bought her one-bedroom-plus study in Casa Delmar three years ago, only to discover hours before she was due to settle that her deposit money was missing.

“On the day I was due to settle, I woke up with my family celebrating ‘settlement day’ on my first home,” said Sudol, a real estate agent for the past 10 years at Stone Real Estate. “I’m baffled and severely disappointed at the lack of accountability over these deposits held by the law firm. In real estate we are so accountable in terms of how trust accounts are managed.” First home buyer Lauren Sodol is outraged after her deposit went missing. Domain Landmark Group is expected to ask the Law Society of NSW to cover outstanding costs via its compensation fund. The fund is capped at $1 million payable on all claims against a law firm. “People are understandably extremely distressed the deposits they have worked so hard to save have gone missing,” a spokesperson for the NSW government said. “This a serious matter which is before the courts and we hope it can be resolved as quickly as possible.”

David Winning, founder and head of YM Conveyancing, has four clients who bought apartments in the Dee Why development whose purchases have been delayed. “As far as we are concerned, the contract between buyers and the developer is still legally enforceable,” Winning said. “While the issue of settlement and the deposit funds is a matter for the courts, technically the developer is in breach of contract for not settling.” Winning said there would be ancillary costs to account for through this process as buyers are left with removalist and rent costs while they can’t move into their homes.

“Investors will also have mounting costs as they will be unable to rent out apartments,” Winning said. Unemployment in Melbourne’s outer western suburbs has climbed to its highest level since the depths of the pandemic as higher interest rates and inflation combine to weaken the jobs market and squeeze family budgets. Even as evidence grow that the AI data construction boom is approaching levels not seen since the mining boom of the early 2010s, figures from the Bureau of Statistics show that in the Wyndham area the unemployment rate has reached 8 per cent, with surrounding suburbs not far behind. In Wyndham, which covers suburbs including Hoppers Crossing, Werribee and Wyndham Vale, the number of people out of work has climbed by 3500 over the past 12 months. Michael Howard The national unemployment rate reached 4.9 per cent in October, with the country shedding almost 80,000 jobs over the past two months. Despite inflation hitting 4.9 per cent in October, financial markets believe the Reserve Bank will start cutting interest rates from August to support the rapidly softening jobs market. This week, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said his mid-year budget update will show that Treasury expects unemployment is likely to climb above 5 per cent in 2027.

Advertisement

The combination of high unemployment and inflation has sharply lifted pressure on Chalmers to unveil spending cuts in next month’s budget update, with the opposition demanding the treasurer be sacked. The regional unemployment figures from the bureau highlight that parts of the country are already dealing with job losses before the full impact of the Reserve Bank’s most recent rate hikes filter through the economy. In Wyndham, which covers suburbs including Hoppers Crossing, Werribee and Wyndham Vale, the number of people out of work has climbed by 3500 or more than 27 per cent over the past 12 months. The jobless rate in the area had fallen to 6.4 per cent in December, but it has spiralled to 8 per cent since the RBA started tightening monetary policy.

Advertisement

In neighbouring Brimbank, the unemployment rate has climbed to 6.7 per cent from 5.6 per cent, with the number of people out of work climbing by a fifth or 1300 people. Melbourne’s south-east suburbs are not being spared, with the jobless rate in the southern parts of the Casey area jumping to 7.2 per cent. In Casey’s northern suburbs, unemployment has also lifted, from 5.3 per cent to 6.4 per cent. The western suburbs of both Sydney and Melbourne are exposed most to the sharp lift in interest rates and inflation. High petrol prices, which have climbed by more than a third since the start of the war against Iran, have delivered particular financial pain. The highest unemployment rate is in Chalmers’ seat of Rankin, hitting 8.7 per cent in the suburbs of Springwood and Kingston. A year ago, the jobless rate in these areas was 7 per cent.

Advertisement

Unemployment is also rising quickly in other parts of Queensland, including Ipswich, Caboolture, the state’s far west and Maryborough. Related Article Analysis

Australian economy Chalmers cannot spin a silver lining out of this grim story Women are paying the highest price for the unemployment increase. Across Melbourne’s western suburbs, the female jobless rate has climbed from 5.8 per cent to 7.8 per cent. Among men, it has risen from 6 per cent to 6.6 per cent. It’s a similar story in Sydney. In Parramatta, female unemployment has climbed by 1.2 percentage points from 5.7 per cent to 6.9 per cent. Among men, the jobless rate in the area is 6 per cent. The increase in unemployment is occurring despite one of the nation’s largest construction booms.

Bureau of Statistics figures released on Thursday showed private spending on new buildings and equipment jumped by 18.6 per cent over the past year. It reached $59.7 billion in the September quarter, the highest level since 2014. In the September quarter alone, capital spending jumped by 12.2 per cent due largely to a 23.1 per cent jump in spending on new equipment and machinery such as computer servers for data centres. It was the single largest quarterly increase since the early stages of last decade’s mining boom. And businesses are not showing signs of plans to slow down. The regional unemployment figures from the bureau highlight that parts of the country are already dealing with job losses before the full impact of the Reserve Bank’s most recent rate increases filter through the economy. A man pushes his shopping trolley containing groceries across the road in Merrylands, Sydney. Kate Geraghty In the Merrylands-Guildford area, unemployment has jumped from 6.5 per cent in October last year to 7.8 per cent this year, the highest rate in Sydney. The total number of people out of work there has climbed by almost a quarter, or 1300 people, with most of the deterioration in the jobs market occurring since the RBA started lifting interest rates in February. Just to the south, unemployment has climbed to 7.3 per cent in Fairfield after being at 6.9 per cent in October last year. Further west, in Mount Druitt, the jobless rate has increased to 7.1 per cent from 6.5 per cent.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Australian economy Chalmers cannot spin a silver lining out of this grim story Outside of Sydney, the unemployment rate has increased above 6 per cent in regional and remote areas including Bourke, Inverell and Moree. The western suburbs of Sydney and Melbourne are exposed most to the sharp lift in interest rates and inflation. High petrol prices, which have climbed by more than a third since the start of the war against Iran, have delivered particular financial pain. The highest unemployment rate is in Chalmers’ seat of Rankin in Queensland, hitting 8.7 per cent in the suburbs of Springwood and Kingston. A year ago, the jobless rate in these areas was 7 per cent. Unemployment is also lifting quickly in other parts of Queensland, including Ipswich, Caboolture, the state’s far west and Maryborough.

Advertisement

Women are paying the highest price for the unemployment increase. Across Melbourne’s western suburbs, the female jobless rate has climbed from 5.8 per cent to 7.8 per cent. Among men, it has lifted from 6 per cent to 6.6 per cent. It’s a similar story in Sydney. In Parramatta, female unemployment has climbed by 1.2 percentage points from 5.7 per cent to 6.9 per cent. Among men, the jobless rate in the area is 6 per cent. The increase in unemployment is occurring despite one of the nation’s largest construction booms. Bureau of Statistics figures released on Thursday showed private spending on new buildings and equipment jumped by 18.6 per cent over the past year. It reached $59.7 billion in the September quarter, the highest level since 2014.

Advertisement

In the September quarter alone, capital spending jumped by 12.2 per cent due largely to a 23.1 per cent jump in spending on new equipment and machinery such as computer servers for data centres. It was the single largest quarterly increase since the early stages of last decade’s mining boom. And businesses are not showing signs of plans to slow down. Expected spending was lifted by 11.8 per cent to a record $223 billion through 2026-27. NSW and Victoria are attracting the most AI investment, with spending in both lifting by more than a third over the past 12 months. Chalmers described the figures as “absolutely stunning”, saying they confirmed that capital spending by the private sector was booming.

Advertisement

But under pressure from the Coalition over the state of the jobs market, the treasurer admitted the situation was poor. Related Article Inflation Stagflation fears grip Canberra as inflation, unemployment surge “When it comes to the tick-up in unemployment, we have acknowledged that for those Australians who are impacted, then that is very bad development,” he told parliament. AMP economist My Bui said the investment boom in AI-related technology had grown on average by 46 per cent a year since 2001. She said private business investment remained strong despite the lift in interest rates, although that situation could change.

“The outlook for next year will be tougher though, as higher cash rates and bond yields will make it harder for firms to finance their capex plans and the productivity gains from AI are yet to arrive,” she said. Former housing minister Mick de Brenni was effectively “everywhere” in the Queensland Building and Construction Commission’s decision-making, despite no formal ministerial directions ever being issued, an ex-senior building watchdog executive told the CFMEU inquiry on Thursday. Former QBCC licensing director Ian Grant said then-commissioner Brett Bassett described his relationship with de Brenni to him as “one of plausible deniability” – a comment Grant said was made in front of several witnesses. Grant said that culture permeated the upper echelons of the QBCC, in which de Brenni’s name was barely mentioned. Former Labor minister Mick de Brenni. Jamila Filippone Instead, references were made to “the person whose name we cannot mention” and “our political master” – a practice championed by then-deputy commissioner Philip Halton and sometimes adopted by Bassett.

Advertisement

Asked to explain “plausible deniability”, Grant said: “That the minister’s involved, but it’s plausible that you can deny involvement.” “The minister could only direct a commissioner to do something by putting it in writing and tabling it,” he said. “That never occurred, but the minister is everywhere here.” In his witness statement, Grant said Halton, de Brenni’s former chief of staff, advocated wider use of licensing conditions to produce faster regulatory outcomes than traditional enforcement. The most serious allegations centred on a 2019 meeting about possible action against tier-one contractor Watpac, then embroiled in an enterprise bargaining dispute involving the CFMEU and subcontractors over the North Queensland Stadium in Townsville.

Advertisement

Grant said Bassett opened the meeting by saying words to the effect that “the only reason we are here is because an EBA has not been signed”. Grant said he understood the remark as an acknowledgement the QBCC was being drawn into – or “weaponised” in – an industrial dispute. Former Queensland Building and Construction Commission licensing director Ian Grant giving evidence on Thursday, Commission of Inquiry According to Grant, Bassett told him he was pressured from “the very top” to impose a special licence condition forcing Watpac to engage an independent assessor to audit whether all of its subcontractors were appropriately licensed. Grant said he understood “the very top” to mean de Brenni. Grant said he opposed licence conditions on Watpac because the statutory threshold had not been met and told Bassett he could exercise the power himself.

Advertisement

Instead, Grant said, Bassett declined to make the decision personally, saying it “wouldn’t look right” and whoever signed off on it would need “top cover” because “it’s going to blow up”. “It felt like he was giving assurance that he was going to give me top cover, but I was not buying it,” Grant said. While the QBCC fined PJ Walsh $2611 for earlier unlicensed concreting work – a charge director Patrick Walsh rejected after being told twice by the regulator that his builder’s licence covered the work – no regulatory action was taken against Watpac. Later, Walsh told the inquiry he initially did not intend to tender for a stadium contract, as it would have been a union job. “Everyone’s aware in the industry of the fear and intimidation the CFMEU can do to people,” he said.

Advertisement

But tender they did after a Watpac representative assured him it was not a union job, and Walsh said they came to regret it – a campaign of union harassment was to come his way. Related Article Graphic content

CFMEU Secret witness tells inquiry about drug-fuelled sex party on Gold Coast Walsh’s company already had an enterprise agreement with its workers, he said, to which the CFMEU was not a party and had signed a variation under the state government’s Best Practice Principles policy to pay higher state-funded rates without signing a union EBA. “My employees were egged on to put pressure on me to pay them the uplifted wages, or sign the CFMEU EBA agreement,” he said. In July 2020, the Federal Court found the CFMEU and organiser Grant Harradine had organised an illegal four-day walkout by Walsh’s workers in March 2019 to coerce him into signing a union agreement, imposing civil penalties.

Advertisement

In his witness statement, Walsh said the union’s complaint over his concreting licence came less than two weeks after he obtained a Fair Work Commission order halting the strike, leaving him feeling the QBCC was “doing the CFMEU’s bidding” while senior union official Jade Ingham sat on its board. Walsh said the situation deteriorated to the point where he feared for his safety. “One afternoon a private number came up on my phone and I answered it,” he said. “He said he was a detective … and that on a phone-tap they picked up that a hit was being organised on me, and that I should be vigilant about that. “I asked them what they were going to do about it, and they said that they were going to do nothing because they were working a drug case that was unrelated.”

Advertisement

Commissioner Stuart Wood asked how Walsh could try to remain vigilant about a potential hit. Related Article CFMEU Local businesses sidelined by CFMEU demands on major projects “Drink more and try to forget about it and pretend it wasn’t happening, but that only leads to one place,” Walsh replied. Walsh said he has since stayed away from government-funded jobs through fear of union involvement. Grant also told the inquiry a formal QBCC risk-register entry warning of “regulatory capture” was stripped out in 2018 shortly after since-removed CFMEU Queensland assistant secretary Ingham and National Fire Industry Association president Andrew Hickman were appointed to the expanded board.

Advertisement

Grant said Halton summoned him to his office, said the entry was “inappropriate because of the current composition of the board”, ordered it be removed and instructed him to ensure the words “regulatory capture” no longer be used in general communications. There was also a push to strip builders of their licences on fit-and-proper-person grounds over multiple minor workplace safety improvement notices, Grant said – a move he and assistant commissioner Kate Raymond warned was legally unworkable and would have given the union “incredible leverage” to force directors off company boards. Grant resigned in July 2021 after, he said, he was told he and Raymond were on a “hit list” of executives to be removed before Bassett left office and felt senior leadership had betrayed frontline staff. title: Flight Centre hit by cyber incident affecting ‘significant number’ of customers

BusinessCompaniesCybersecurity Flight Centre hit by cyber incident affecting ‘significant number’ of customers Chris Zappone and David Swan Updated November 26, 2026 — 4:31pm ,first published 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Major travel agency Flight Centre has warned the accommodation booking system it uses has been affected by “unusual” cyber activity involving a large number of customer records and “limited passport details”. Brisbane-based Flight Centre said while investigations remain ongoing, it believes “that a significant number of customer records in the impacted system may have been accessed by unknown persons”. Flight Centre has disclosed an incident affecting its third-party hotel booking platform. Eamon Gallagher The company said it remained unclear “how many of those records have actually been extracted” from the third-party booking system Flight Centre uses, but most of the accessed records include “only customer names”, some with basic travel information. “A very small percentage is believed to include data such as limited passport details, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, or in rare cases health or mobility information,” Flight Centre said in a statement to the ASX, without naming the accommodation booking provider.

Advertisement

The incident appears to affect the accommodation system used by Flight Centre and travel brands Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent agents. To date, Flight Centre said no customer credit cards, payments or bank account details have been identified as accessed, and flight bookings have not been affected either. Related Article Updated

Aviation Virgin in talks with Boeing, Airbus as it looks to order more planes Flight Centre said it was working with its cybersecurity partner Mandiant “to understand the nature and extent of the activity and to implement appropriate safeguards and containment action”. With Google-subsidiary, Mandiant, the company is working to “contain the activity, change authentication keys and credentials”, it said. Mandiant and Flight Centre have also increased the monitoring on the system. Flight Centre did not say how many customers were affected, when the activity was detected or whether any of the data had surfaced online. The company was contacted for further comment.

Advertisement

Its shares fell about 2 per cent on Thursday. David Hayes, regional vice-president for Asia Pacific and Japan at cybersecurity company Arctic Wolf, said the involvement of an outside booking platform showed some of a company’s biggest vulnerabilities “may lie outside of its own four walls”. “From an attacker’s perspective, why target businesses individually when compromising a single technology provider could potentially expose the customer data of multiple organisations,” he said. The use of third-party contractors in the travel sector has exposed travel-related companies to cyber incidents before. Last year, hackers accessed 5.7 million Qantas customers records through a Philippines call centre contracted by the airlines. The data then included information on frequent flyer accounts, addresses and even the food preferences of thousands of travellers.

Advertisement

The incident saw detailed loyalty program data, including membership in Qantas’ exclusive Chairman’s Lounge, purloined by hacking group Scattered Spider. Qantas customers were caught up again last month after Spanish travel technology provider Amadeus, whose booking systems are used by hotels, travel companies and more than 400 airlines, told affected carriers in late October it had suffered a breach. In April, Booking.com warned customers that unauthorised parties had accessed reservation details including names, email addresses and phone numbers. Samuel Spencer, an adjunct professor of data governance at the University of Canberra, said Flight Centre was the latest travel business hit through its supply chain. “The rise of software as a service provides business with the opportunity to bring new capabilities in quickly, but at the end of the day, it’s their name that customers see,” he said. Spencer said companies needed vendors to spell out who could access their data and where it was stored. “Anyone who can’t answer that and put it in a contract shouldn’t be trusted for sensitive information,” he said.

Advertisement

It is not Flight Centre’s first privacy lapse. In 2017, the company gave participants in a “design jam” event a data file containing more than 6 million customer records, some with passport details that consultants had typed into a free-text field. The privacy commissioner later found the company had interfered with customers’ privacy. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.
